to the young in spirit – the youngest volunteer at 21, the young in spirit but more mature at 70. i can tell you that meeting these people makes me enormously proud to be the european commissioner for humanitarian aid because what we are demonstrating is that it is not by chance that europe is a global leader in this field. to be specific concerning parliamentʼs contributions, let me just highlight a few of them: parliament has placed promoting active european citizenship among the initiativeʼs objectives and also measures on communications and visibility that would support this objective and make it happen. parliament has reinforced security of the volunteers as a priority, and on that basis we have excluded deploying eu aid volunteers in theatres of armed conflict. we have placed the emphasis instead on volunteer work in disaster risk reduction and resilience, linking relief to rehabilitation and development. these are entirely aligned with eu priorities but are also fields where there is a shortage of skills in humanitarian organisations. last but not least, parliament has promoted the gender dimension in cooperation with women and i can tell you that every time i go to areas affected by disasters or by conflict i often see women not just as victims but as victors, as those who are saving lives. let me finish by saying that we recognise that we are at the beginning of the process of making this initiative happen, and we look forward to working continuously with parliament in the implementation of the programme, in the adoption of delegated acts, on standards for eu aid volunteersʼ management, on the mid-term review of thematic priorities and financial allocations, as ms[nbsp ]striffler emphasised, and also on the annual report on implementation and in evaluations.

mr president, on 6 february last, 15 migrants drowned a few metres from the beach at tarajal in ceuta, as a result of disproportionate action and, more seriously, in breach of spanish, european and international law. the attitude of the spanish government, which has tried to conceal the use of rubber balls against people trying to reach the coast, is unacceptable. it is intolerable that intercepted migrants are returned 'hot' without being identified or checked for asylum. we therefore call on the european commission to take responsibility for this very serious violation of human rights and of the community acquis itself. we urge the commission to respond to this humanitarian tragedy and to take urgent and effective action. we call on the european union to respond to the increased migratory pressure on the southern states with a solidarity-based migration policy; to increase cooperation; to combat the human trafficking mafias; and to strengthen frontex and the alert mechanisms. in short, an immigration policy that is not exclusively a closed door.
mr president, the multinational coca cola is restructuring in spain: it is closing several factories. coca cola has made 900 million euros in the last year and after half a century of refreshing in spain now closes four factories - 250 layoffs, some relocations, definitive and non-negotiable closure in madrid, asturias, baleares and alicante. coca-cola says, "they are not our employees, there is no contractual relationship". this is how he says goodbye to half a century of working relationship with these people. run and close, and relocate. this is not industrial policy; this is not trade policy. the commission must play the role of industrial policy, and of course coca cola is not going to close or lay off people, because it will lose the spark of life.
mr president, every year, about 3 000 women die in europe as a result of gender-based violence. the figure is brutal, but it's only an estimate. many member states lack statistics because gender-based violence is a private domestic matter in those countries, and it is therefore impossible to combat this scourge. we need a european framework that makes the scale of this problem visible throughout europe, and we must now move to put the figures and the limitation of fundamental rights into practice. we need a comprehensive european strategy focused on victim care, the coordinated prosecution of these crimes and, above all, prevention. gender-based violence is the most serious consequence of inequality, and eradicating it is a matter of education and values. the house of freedom and the values we build every day must, first of all, protect coexistence and respect in every european home for every european woman.

the rapporteur. - mr barroso, i listened to you very carefully today and i would like to believe in the reality you have sweetened today when you talk about improvements, turning points and the way out of the crisis. i'd like to believe you. but after this political-fiction speech that you've addressed us here today, it would be grossly irresponsible to believe every word of it, every diagnosis of it. mr president, i will not deny that there are some positive figures, but can we talk about improvements, mr barroso, with annual growth in 2013 of 0.0%? can we talk about improvements with 27 million unemployed in europe (one in five young people unemployed)? can we talk about improvements when 24 per cent of european households and families are at risk of poverty, at risk of social exclusion? can we talk about recovery when, after having injected 500 billion euros into the financial system, credit still does not flow and the little that does does so at totally exorbitant interest rates? no, mr barroso, i have not. if we are talking about improvements in the financing systems of the member states, i welcome it. if we do it by talking about trade deficits, i do the same. but to proclaim recovery today with this rate of growth, unemployment and inequality seems to me a serious exercise of irresponsibility on your part. but you know what the bigger problem is, mr. president? the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we are in the europe of divergences, in the europe of inequality, in a europe which, in order to emerge from the crisis, is losing every single one of the signs of identity that we have built with this project. or can you, mr barroso, be proud that for the first time in european history the levels of convergence between member states are declining today? or can he be proud that the gap between the rich and the poor in the european union today is widening like never before? or can we be proud that the gap in unemployment growth rates between the peripheral and central countries is the largest in our history (10.5 points in 2012 and still growing)? or can we be proud that 20 of the 28 member states have cut their budgets for education today and that we are giving up human capital 'just to compete on the downside at costs which, by the way, are no longer worthwhile and which are putting our social model at risk'? mr barroso, in the report i am rapporteur for we warn of the lack of commitment of the commission and the member states to the recommendations made by this european parliament, and that is why we are calling for an interinstitutional agreement to go further. we remind him of the recessive effects of the deficit reduction timetable on growth and employment, but we also warn him that some of the structural reforms the commission is proposing may be as harmful to growth as that timetable for fiscal reduction has been. we ask you to strengthen the social indicators, which have taken four years to introduce and are now insufficient when it comes to making your recommendations. we ask them to create a real investment package to compensate in part for the excesses of adjustment that are being imposed in some countries of the european union and, above all, we ask them for a more ambitious strategy to fight for employment and against youth unemployment. but most of all, we tell them they're right. we tell them that we cannot fall into complacency and that we must continue to make improvements that increase our competitiveness. but that cannot be achieved solely and exclusively by devaluing wages: firstly, because we are devaluing our domestic demand, because it makes us more dependent on the economic conditions of other countries; but, above all, what they are doing to us is increasing the feeling of social injustice of many citizens who either lose their jobs or lose a significant part of their wages. i would like to conclude, mr president, by reminding you that a few weeks ago the commission warned that in some countries of the european union today having a salary is no longer synonymous with getting out of poverty. or rather, that the wages earned for their work are no longer sufficient to guarantee a minimum of decent quality of life. what i am wondering is whether the commission, whether you, mr barroso, are aware that it is your policies, your recommendations, your decisions that are promoting precisely what you are criticizing.
mr president, commission president, minister, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur for the committee on economic and monetary affairs, mr de backer, on the great work he has done on this report. i believe that this debate on the european semester is an opportunity to take stock of what has been achieved so far. as president barroso said, a little over a year ago we were talking about the collapse of the euro. the debate today is about growth and job creation, and above all how to accelerate the latter. all this has been achieved thanks to the efforts of everyone, thanks to reforms at national level, thanks to the processes of fiscal consolidation and thanks to the progress in european integration. however, as we said here, much remains to be done. no one's said otherwise. the focus now needs to be on boosting growth and job creation, and to do this it is key to continue the reform processes at national level in order to achieve productivity gains and to continue to boost our exports, which will undoubtedly be the engine of growth. but above all, more effort is needed to ensure that smes have access to credit. it is true that the banking union and the single resolution mechanism will help to achieve this objective, but it is not enough. in the short term we need stronger action from the european investment bank and the european central bank, and we also need to join forces to fight youth unemployment. i would like to highlight the efforts made by commissioner andor in this respect. it's time to release the juvenile bond funds. they need to be active as soon as possible. finally, we must continue to move towards the much-needed economic and monetary union with greater democratic legitimacy.
mr president, commissioners, mr minister, a year ago we debated the direction of the political guidelines of the european union and the need or not to change the economic and social strategy. two options were considered: to continue with fiscal and budgetary consolidation that was proportional, differentiated and favourable to growth, or to return to the path of those policies based on spending which had led us to a situation of crisis, unemployment and social drama. fortunately, we have opted for the former and, despite the efforts of the citizens, the situation is changing. the economic scenario - the starting point for steady and secure progress in job creation - and the social situation have improved. we have overcome the doubts and fears about the possible bankruptcy of some countries or the break-up of the euro. and we have secured the welfare state and social services that the wrong policies of the past have put in jeopardy. the fruits are beginning to be seen, the job destruction has stopped and we are on the path of growth - little by little - and the recovery of employment. so now, with the economic outlook improving, it is time to focus more deeply on the social and employment aspects - without changing course and continuing in the reformist spirit - and, above all, on the labour market. nor can we forget the particular needs of certain regions or provinces, especially those with a low population density where it is more difficult to maintain economic activity and therefore employment, which affects the provision of public services such as education or health care. in spain there are several regions which suffer from this problem, such as my own region, aragon, and in particular the province of teruel. i therefore ask that in future this problem be taken into account in the allocation of the cohesion funds, as has been done in the northern regions of europe with such good results.
the rapporteur. - mr president, i should like to begin by thanking all the speakers and by stressing something that has been mentioned here: the complementarity of the three reports. the three of them bring together the reality of a european economy which, while it is true that it has made improvements from a macroeconomic point of view, also has a dramatic social aspect. the problem with mr barroso's speech today is that he wanted to emphasize the first too much, whilst completely ignoring the second; and ignoring reality does not make the problems disappear, but on the contrary, makes them worse. mr barroso and many other members of the pp today wanted to talk to us about the benefits of fiscal consolidation, but they defend it with some statements that are not true. mr barroso said that there are some who still defend the deficit today ('spend what you don't have') and that is not true. what we are advocating is precisely another pace of fiscal consolidation which is radically the opposite. why would you do that? because there are studies which are telling us that a different pace of fiscal consolidation would have prevented, in percentage terms, much more job destruction than some of the labour reforms which are being done and which the commission is so much promoting in this european semester process. look, the most alarming thing is that we created this half-year process to increase coordination of economic policies, to boost growth and foster cohesion. and the reality is that, four years later, we have only had one single recipe that has not exactly favoured economic growth, it has increased economic divergences and, above all, social inequalities. and it is now our responsibility to be able to correct them, by considering the social and employment elements on an equal footing with the macroeconomic ones, by an action aimed at stimulating knowledge, by restructuring private debt - to which no one has referred today - which is as alarming and more worrying in terms of sustainability, for example, than public debt, and also by making a real investment plan. i would also like to thank the work of the alternative rapporteurs, the other rapporteurs on the other reports and, above all, ana ahijado, because without her work i would certainly not have been able to produce this report of which i am so proud.

in writing. - in favour. the european police office (europol) was established in the first instance on 26 july 1995 by a convention, the only instrument available at that point in time under the maastricht treaty. the convention had to be ratified by all member states before it entered into force. this meant that the europol convention could only be altered through a ‘protocol’, an instrument which then had to be submitted to the national parliaments for its subsequent ratification. three protocols were ratified between 2000 and 2003, with the aim of improving europol’s operation. these protocols entered into force between 29 march and 18 april 2007. the procedure involved was particularly long and complex. this shows the extent to which it was difficult, or almost impossible, to rapidly alter europol’s overall framework to tackle urgent situations for which it required new powers. europol needed to be governed by a more effective legal instrument that would enable it to respond more rapidly in its fight against crime, with the latter taking on an ever more international character.

in writing. - in favour. through the europe 2020 strategy, the european union has set itself the target of reducing the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion by at least 20 million by 2020. the economic and financial crisis ,however, is exacerbating poverty and social exclusion across the union. almost 120 million europeans, a rise of six million in two years and now nearly one quarter of the total population, were at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2011. over 40 million suffer from severe material deprivation. one in ten under 60-year olds live in households with low-work intensity. one of the main features of material deprivation is an inability to access appropriate quantities and qualities of food. 43 million europeans are unable to afford a meal with meat, chicken or fish (or vegetarian equivalent) every second day, a who-defined basic need. children are particularly sensitive to food poverty and poor eating patterns can adversely affect brain development and capacity to learn as well as their future health.

on behalf of the s&d group, madam president, dear rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, the accessibility directive is intended to ensure that the content of public sector websites or websites operated by bodies performing public functions is accessible to all users, in particular to the group of people with disabilities, whether physical, mental, intellectual or sensory. this group - as has already been said - is estimated to represent some 80 million people in the european union as a whole. a broad range of public services is established to help member states meet their commitments: energy services, postal services, electronic communications networks, transport services, basic banking and insurance services, education, social protection, health, childcare, cultural and tourist activities. this directive will give citizens a greater ability to integrate fully in society and in their professional lives and to exercise their right of access to information. this directive will remove barriers to the internal market, reducing its fragmentation and increasing the confidence of suppliers and users. the websites concerned are expected to guarantee the neutrality of the network and its accessibility free of charge, as well as the security of information transmission and the protection of personal data. the directive emphasises accessibility irrespective of the device used, including mobile devices. the time limits for compliance with this directive are gradual. it shall apply in full between one and three years after the date of its entry into force. member states shall lay down rules on penalties applicable in an effective, proportionate and dissuasive manner in the event of non-compliance. we are laying the foundations for improving the quality of life, guaranteeing the basic rights of particularly vulnerable sections of the european population.

mr president, commissioner andor, we need the integration of young people into the labour market, but we also need clear criteria and fraud prevention in order to apply european funds; we need to increase public and private collaboration; we need to share good practice, because we cannot let young people down and because our economy and competitiveness need their talent. they are the source of excellence and innovation for our growth. it is the states that must put forward the plans. you have spoken of 19 states which have raised them. i would like to ask you what your assessment is of the plans that have been put forward and what is the position of the eight that have not yet reacted immediately. do these plans include the regions? because the basque country has young people with a very qualified education and needs that are different from those of other spanish regions. has the spanish state presented its plan? and i would like to ask you: in the quality framework, a big disappointment. the states are opposing, as you have said. what are the arguments for states to oppose the quality framework we need if we really believe in young people? you asked us for help. how do we think we can help you? i'm willing to do that.

in writing. - the european commission's seventh and eighth progress reports on eu cohesion policy show a widening of development disparities between european regions as a result of the economic crisis. they continue to state that convergence regions are not able to overcome their difficulties on their own and that transition regions must continue their efforts to meet the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy. finally, they believe that interaction between cities and regions should be intensified in the mutual interest of achieving regional growth. once this analysis is established, the draft report makes suggestions to alleviate such problems, such as the continuous monitoring of the implementation of the europe 2020 strategy or investment in infrastructure projects (in particular through support for cohesion policy), warning that the evaluation tools used by the commission are insufficient, and not sufficiently precise, and that the dependence of some member states and regions on the cohesion funds is a cause for concern. in line with the relevance of these measures, i express my support for the report.

in writing. - in favour. the treaty on the functioning of the european union (tfeu) has added a new instrument to the toolbox of budgetary discharge: evaluation of the finances of the union based on results achieved. pursuant to article[nbsp ]318 of the treaty the commission is to prepare an annual report in this respect. since it focuses on financial performance this evaluation report complements the compliance approach developed by the european court of auditors in chapters[nbsp ]1 to 9 of its annual report. it offers parliament the opportunity to assess policy achievements and the legality of financial transactions. this shift will also facilitate the transition from activity-based budgeting to performance-based budgeting.

in writing. - in favour. the european union’s value added tax (vat) is a general, broadly based consumption tax assessed on the value added of all commercial activities involving the production and distribution of goods and the provision of services, apart from few exemptions. vat does normally not apply to goods which are sold for export or services. however, it does apply to imports, so that eu producers can compete on equal footing in the internal market with suppliers of imported goods and services that are based outside of the union. vat is an indirect tax which is ultimately borne by the final consumer. it is charged as a percentage of the price paid by the buyer to the seller and collected through partial payments whereby each taxable person (both vat-registered businesses and self-employed persons) deduct from the vat they have collected the amount of tax they have paid to other taxable persons on purchases for their business activities. this mechanism ensures that the tax is neutral regardless of how many transactions are involved.
in writing. - by council decision 2009/831/ec, portugal was authorised to apply the reduced rate of excise duty in its autonomous regions of madeira and the azores to liqueurs and rums produced and consumed in those regions. this is justified by their small size, their fragmented nature, the low mechanization of their farms and the additional costs linked to the transport to the islands of raw materials not produced locally. since these elements remain unchanged, i welcome the fact that this decision seeks to amend the period of application, so that the deadline is extended from 31 december 2013 to december 2020.

in writing. - by council decision 2004/162/ec of 10 february 2004, france was authorised to apply exemptions or reductions from port taxes for a number of specific products in the overseas regions of guadeloupe, french guiana, martinique and réunion. this is due to the remoteness, isolation, small market and low level of exports of these regions, as these factors, together with the dependence on air and sea transport, energy and raw materials, have a side effect on production costs, so that, without this measure, local production would be unsustainable. this proposal aims to update the decision by adding the region of mayotte, which was classified as an overseas region by decision 2012/419/eu. since the territory of mayotte, as an overseas region, suffers the same disadvantages as the regions already included in the decision, i welcome the fact that it is intended to be added.

in writing. - in favour. more than 8 billion journeys a year are made by rail in europe, and 10 % of goods are transported by rail freight. the sector is responsible for a turnover of eur 73 billion, generating eur 13 billion of revenue and supporting 800 000 jobs. in its white paper entitled ‘roadmap to a single european transport area – towards a competitive and resource efficient transport system’, the commission sets out its belief that, by 2050, more than half of medium-distance passenger and freight transport will be by rail. as well as improving choice for users and opportunities for entrepreneurs, this objective is essential if, by 2050, we are to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 20 % and co2 emissions by 60 % compared to 1990 levels. by comparing the objectives with the current situation we can see the growth potential in an industry in which european manufacturers are world leaders in technology, particularly when it comes to safety and high speed trains.

mr president, we know the speed and development of the digital age and the increase in public sector websites, which must be adapted to the needs of europeans and provide up-to-date information and services to all equally. however, only 10[nbsp ]% of current european union websites are accessible in accordance with accessibility standards. today, the european union market for website accessibility provides jobs for one million people. it is therefore a priority to enable all people, including people with disabilities, to use websites. i welcome the improvements introduced by the report adopted today: the extension of the scope of the public websites directive to include mobile devices. member states are obliged to train their staff on accessibility requirements. consequently, sanctions may be imposed in the event of non-compliance with the new directive. sanctions are necessary when cuts at the beginning of the crisis affect mainly people with disabilities.
in writing. - currently, less than one third of public websites are accessible, while more than 60%[nbsp ] of the european population access the internet daily. the new legislation will benefit not only the 80 million european citizens with disabilities, but also the 87 million over 65 as well as many citizens without high ict skills. furthermore, the market for web developers (which provides employment for over a million people) will be able to work across the eu in a harmonised internal market and governments will not need to establish alternative means of obtaining information or services due to the inaccessibility of their web pages. i consider this directive, which i have participated in by submitting multiple amendments, to be very positive, as it will not only put an end to this unequal situation, but will also allow the eu to meet its previous political commitments on web accessibility, such as the 2006 riga ministerial declaration, the digital agenda for europe, the european disability strategy 2010-2020 and the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities, ratified by the eu in 2011.
in writing. - in favour. information and services are increasingly delivered online in the digital age. the quantity of public and private sector websites is therefore growing rapidly. today, there are already over 761[nbsp ]000 public sector websites offering access to information and services alone. however, currently less than 10[nbsp ]% of websites in the eu are accessible by web-accessibility standards. the eu market for web-accessibility consists of more than 175[nbsp ]000 companies. the turnover generated by the approximately one million people working in the web development industry is estimated at around eur[nbsp ]144 billion. the economic impact for the eu, as well as the large gap that exists with non-accessible websites, makes web-accessibility a lucrative business in the social area with significant potential for growth and inclusiveness. thus, web accessibility can further develop the single market and extensively make services available to all eu citizens. web accessibility is vital as it makes websites usable for all people, including those with disabilities. public sector bodies and any entities providing basic services to the public must adopt the inclusive practice of web accessibility to fulfil their responsibility towards all citizens.
in writing. - in favour. long-term investment is key for economic growth and job creation. without it, crucial projects in the areas of infrastructure, research and development, and innovation cannot be started or carried out successfully. right now almost all european countries are pursuing a policy of fiscal consolidation to get a grip on their debt. while sound fiscal policies serve as the underlying foundation, it is crucial that europe enters a path of sustainable growth that enhances its competitiveness vis-à-vis other global regions and ensures the creation of jobs. financing of the real economy plays a pivotal role in the process, yet currently faces significant obstacles in europe. in times of stressed financial markets, mainly due to the ongoing global financial crisis and the unresolved sovereign debt crisis, europe’s traditionally high reliance on funding through banks has proven to be a major impediment to the intermediation process of allocating funds. not only has high risk aversion dried up the supply of finance, but it also prevents necessary investment from being undertaken and as a result brings the economic recovery process to a standstill.
in writing. - we start from the premise that sexual exploitation of persons, trafficking in human beings and trafficking in women must be tackled with toughness and tenacity, and that this requires the development of common and coordinated policies at european union level. but we do not believe that the philosophy behind the resolution is the right one. we do not believe that the so-called nordic model, which is promoted in the resolution and is based on illegalization and repression, is the most appropriate way of dealing with the issue of prostitution and eliminating the sexual exploitation of people. we think that the nordic model hides prostitution, eliminates it from the public space, but does not eliminate its practice. this creates opaque spaces that can lead to increased sexual exploitation, with greater risk and less protection for those who practice it. we are in favour of a policy of legalising and decriminalising the practice of prostitution, while at the same time promoting the recognition of the labour and social rights of those engaged in it. i therefore call for a vote on the alternative motion tabled by several political groups which, by calling for the fight against sexual exploitation, trafficking and trafficking in women, does not promote the nordic model and leaves the door open to other types of proposals.
in writing. - against. i am one of the co-sponsors of the alternative resolution that favours making a difference between forced prostitution and prostitution resulting from individual choice. forced prostitution, human trafficking and sexual exploitation need to be combated by all means necessary. but sex workers who choose to do this work need to be offered healthcare, protection, empowerment and the chance to do their work legally, while all who make the individual choice to leave prostitution need to be offered all social and educational opportunities to do so. the meps who support the alternative resolution are convinced that this is the best way to ensure sex workers get the protection and assistance they need, and to ensure victims of forced prostitution and trafficking feel they can report to the police. criminalising sex work will have the opposite effect. it adds to the social stigma of sex workers and forces them to go underground, making them more vulnerable to violence and exploitation instead of less. criminalising also makes the threshold for victims of trafficking and exploitation to report to the police even higher and means less access for sex workers to healthcare and contraceptives, making them more vulnerable to sexually transmitted diseases.
in writing. - without prejudice to policies against trafficking and sexual crime, the possibility of establishing a regulatory framework for the practice of prostitution should be considered, so that those men and women who freely and without coercion decide to engage in prostitution can do so with full legal certainty, with the necessary health and hygiene guarantees and with a clear statute containing the appropriate rights and obligations.
in writing. - in favour. countries with a long history of mineral imports, such as the united states, japan and european countries, are experiencing growing competition over access to and security of supply of strategic mineral resources. this situation offers developing countries the opportunity to capitalise on their natural resource endowments. while the world’s unprecedented demand for minerals and other natural resources represents a unique chance to enable mining to contribute to sustainable development, it also poses major challenges for developing countries. the exploitation of high-value natural resources, including oil, gas, minerals and timber, is a major source of conflicts around the world, especially in a context where increasing competition over diminishing renewable resources, such as land and water, is on the rise. this is being further aggravated by environmental degradation, population growth and climate change. the mismanagement of land and natural resources is contributing to new conflicts and obstructing the peaceful resolution of existing ones.

not even a month since i last stood here. we have all followed the tragic developments unfolding before our eyes in the intervening period. what i retain is a sense of immense sorrow over the high numbers of dead and wounded. i wish to express our sympathy and condolences to the families of all those who have fallen victim to what have been unprecedented levels of violence, provocation and indiscriminate use of force in ukraine during the past few weeks. during my last visit to kiev, i visited two hospitals to show solidarity with the injured people. irrespective of which side they were on, they were suffering because of the actions or non-actions of politicians. as president barroso said in this house yesterday, the winds of change are knocking again at ukraine’s doors; the will of the people must prevail. those who violated fundamental rights are to be brought to justice. justice should be fair and without revenge, fully in line with the european convention on human rights and the case[nbsp ]law of the european court of human rights. this tragedy puts an even greater responsibility on all involved to make things work now in ukraine. it places greater responsibility on the meeting in brussels and maintaining regular contact with our colleagues on the ground. we adopted strongly worded council conclusions introducing targeted sanctions. meanwhile, our three colleagues facilitated talks between the president and the opposition in kiev, transmitting the clear and unequivocal messages from the european union. a multi-party delegation from this house, led by the chair of the committee on foreign affairs, elmar[nbsp ]brok, visited kiev over last weekend to meet with counterparts in the verkhovna rada and other stakeholders. it is now important that all sides continue engaging in a meaningful dialogue to fulfil the aspirations of the ukrainian people. we expect everyone in ukraine to behave responsibly and to protect the unity, sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the country. due respect for its regional, cultural and linguistic diversity is also of the utmost importance. we need a lasting solution to the political crisis. elements of that solution are clear, and were outlined in the agreement of 21[nbsp ]february. first, a comprehensive constitutional reform to be started immediately and completed by september, drawing substantially on relevant expertise of the venice commission; second, the formation of a new inclusive government; and third, ensuring the conditions for free and fair elections, also in close cooperation with the venice commission and with the organisation for security and cooperation in europe. i want to underline the importance of the verkhovna rada as a legitimate political institution. it is also crucial that the new administration is inclusive, politically, geographically and in terms of stakeholder participation. as i said earlier, issues such as the investigation of major cases of violence, judicial reform and police reform will have to be addressed in order to heal the wounds of the last days, months and years, and to bring the country forward. we are ready to step in where requested to do so, in close cooperation with our international partners. i welcome the engagement of the council of europe, including commissioner for human rights muižnieks’ recent preliminary report, following his visit to kiev, which focuses on the need to prevent further violence and to ensure that human rights violations are investigated. i also strongly hope that an international advisory panel will start work soon. our offer of political association and economic integration remains on the table and, as stated in our february foreign affairs council conclusions, the association agreement/ deep and comprehensive free trade agreement does not constitute the final goal in eu-ukraine cooperation. we are ready to work promptly with a future ukrainian government committed to economic and political reforms, and to step in with assistance. we are working on the best inclusive platform for international coordination to provide sustainable economic and financial support, including all international partners, to help in addressing the challenges the country faces. baroness ashton was in kiev on monday and tuesday for talks with all the stakeholders present and to engage in the inclusive political process. her visit was warmly welcomed by interlocutors from all political factions and by representatives of maidan. she underlined the need to restore trust in the institutions and reiterated the european union’s offer of help. all partners responded positively to that offer. while in kiev she also met with yulia tymoshenko, released from prison after two-and-a-half years of detention. i spoke to ms[nbsp ]tymoshenko by phone shortly after her release, underlining the importance of her health recovery. her release was an important step forward, given our long-standing concerns about selective justice in ukraine. let me once again thank parliament for its immense efforts on this issue, and let me commend, in particular, the outstanding work done over a sustained period by pat cox and alexander kwaśniewski. before concluding, allow me to say a few words about russia. ukraine needs russia, and russia needs ukraine. russia has a chance to become part of the effort to bring stability and prosperity back to ukraine, including being part of the coordinated international effort to help ukraine address its economic challenges. this will require recognition of the sovereign right of the ukrainian people to make their own choices about their future. those choices are about domestic politics just as much as they are about foreign policy. russia can only gain from ukraine’s success, and it risks losing heavily if ukraine fails. we are ready to work very closely with russia, the neighbour of our neighbour, to ensure it plays a constructive role in ukraine’s future – the future of a neighbour with whom russia has traditional ties, which we support. madam president, honourable members, in the light of the challenges and the need for a continued coherent european policy on ukraine, i congratulate you for organising today’s debate. the european parliament’s involvement has been very important for all in ukraine who have been striving for a stable, prosperous and democratic future.

member of the commission. - madam president, i would like to deliver this answer on behalf of my colleague, commissioner damanaki, who unfortunately was not able to attend today’s sitting. first i would like to thank mr wałęsa for drawing attention to these important questions. let me underline the sensitivity of this important fishery-related issue. it concerns delicate aspects of international law and, more importantly, has a bearing on our relations with norway which, at present and historically, has been our most important partner in fisheries and also other marine-related, including arctic, issues. it has been a consistent position of the european union that the european union member states which are party to the 1920 treaty of paris relating to spitsbergen (svalbard) enjoy the same access rights as other parties to that treaty. as regards fishery management measures, acceptance by the european union of fishery regulations proposed by norway pertaining to the waters around svalbard has been conditional on the regulations being applied in a non-discriminatory manner, based on scientific advice, and respected by all interested parties. with regard to questions 2, 3 and 4 formulated by the honourable member of the european parliament, there is no established european union position on those yet. the implications of the newly drawn ‘murmansk line’ for fisheries in the waters in question are still being considered within different commission departments. finally, the commission is unaware of the procedures by which the norway-russian federation joint fisheries commission operates. the joint fisheries commission is a bilateral arrangement. it is not classified as a regional fisheries management arrangement and the commission does not contemplate participating in its meetings. the commission is unaware of any appropriation of greenland halibut or redfish quotas in the area, so it has no opinion on this matter.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, i would like to congratulate mr wałęsa on his initiative to ensure that our fishing rights in svalbard are not forgotten. this is a matter that has been dragging on for too long and remains unclear, as we have seen tonight. i would like to ask the commission whether in the recent negotiations for the revision of the fisheries agreement with norway, the community negotiator has engaged in any kind of conversation or negotiation to improve the conditions for by-catch of haddock in svalbard and to get rid of norwegian interference in the fishing of our cod quotas in exchange for - and i stress this - the european union giving up its claim to other fishing rights. it is a bigger issue, because, however welcome these improvements may be, other very important rights for other fleets would be left unfulfilled. since both the member states concerned and the commission itself have so far shared the view that norway's interpretation of the paris treaty and the consequences of the creation of the fisheries protection area are contrary to international law and the law of the sea, i would like to know where this initiative to negotiate the future of our quotas in svalbard comes from, how far the terms of this offer go, whether the commission has discussed this with the member states beforehand and whether it has a mandate to conduct such negotiations. i would remind you that norway's uncompromising position was based on the fact that the commission is not a signatory to the paris treaty and would therefore only negotiate with the member states, which the commission in turn prevents from negotiating quotas bilaterally, considering that this is its exclusive competence. i would therefore like the commission to answer all these questions which have recently arisen in the last negotiations with norway and have caused a great deal of consternation both in the member states and in the community fisheries sector.

the next item is the debate on the report by mrs dolores garcía-hierro and mr raül romeva i rueda, on behalf of the committee on fisheries and the committee on women's rights and gender equality, on specific measures in the field of the common fisheries policy to develop the role of women (2013/2150 (ini)) (a7-0070/2014).
the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is almost two years since i began work on the own-initiative report on the recognition of the role of women in the common fisheries policy. first of all, i would like to thank the efforts and collaboration of the officials of the committee on fisheries, my assistant ana and the organisations of women fishermen in europe, who have been fighting since 2006 to ensure that the member states of the european union make visible and recognise the economic, social and cultural contribution made by women in the fishing sector. after a lot of hard work, which was also supported by the committee on women's rights, we have come to a common text which is being presented today. today, if parliament votes in favour of this report, it will be beginning a process of urging the commission and the member states to put an end to this injustice. the lack of economic, labour and social recognition that women fishermen, shellfish farmers, packers, etc. have been suffering. it is not fair that in the 21st century more than 100 000 women - estimated to be in all of europe, since there are no reliable statistics - continue to be denied recognition for the economic and social activity they carry out. their work not only enables them and their families or partners to survive, but also contributes to the sustainability of the environment, the marine environment, small-scale coastal fishing and the towns and regions of europe that live mainly from this activity. we therefore call on the commission to implement, together with the member states of the union, the principle of equality by facilitating women's access to social security, health care, parental leave, unemployment protection and vocational training, as well as the recognition of the specific pathologies or diseases they suffer from carrying out this activity. in short, they should be able to enjoy a salary and all the other legal, labour and social rights, just like men. we urge the commission and the member states to produce complete, harmonised and accurate statistical information so that we can have accurate and reliable data; to support associations of women fishermen; to facilitate the financing and participation of the european network of women's organisations in fisheries and aquaculture (aktea), so that they can continue their work of training, participation, exchange of proposals and advice to women in the sector. i also think it is essential that the commission and the council encourage the member states to regulate, as far as women fishermen are concerned, specific occupational diseases or injuries from fishing, as they occur as a result of the harsh conditions in which they fish. finally, at a time when we are discussing the trialogue of the european maritime and fisheries fund, i would like to see the financing of the projects mentioned above made possible through this instrument and also to facilitate women and young women's access to vocational training and vocational training, to setting up businesses or to being self-employed, to obtaining micro-credits, to carrying out this economic activity which is so important in the fisheries sector. these regions, ladies and gentlemen, are becoming known to us all mainly because of this invisible work of women. that is why i ask for your vote in favour.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. i must say that the debate is not new to me, because i have been working in the two committees responsible for this issue - the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities and the committee on fisheries - in that regard. so in a way what this report does is to merge two of the - for me - big issues that are currently holding our attention. it is also important to highlight the fact that many colleagues have been working on this issue for a long time, as we have seen in some of the trips we have made in the past - thanks to our colleague izaskun bilbao - to the basque country, where we were able to get to know the reality of many of these organisations, many of these women who clearly demanded greater visibility and greater recognition of their activity. so what this report is about is simply to do justice to all those people, all those women, all those organisations who have done a clearly invisible job in those last few years - not recognised, not socially, not economically, not legally - and who therefore needed to be compensated in some way. over 100 000 women work in different aspects of the fishing sector: 4% in the extractive fishing sector (work related to fishing vessels, such as rowing, packing or packing); 30% in the aquaculture sector (mainly shellfish) and 60% - the vast majority - in the processing industry. the hard work they do clearly demands attention which has not been given to them until now. (interruption by the president) i have had the opportunity to experience this hard work and hardship personally. in this report, therefore, we are urging the commission, but also the other bodies of the european union, to change the situation, starting with the recognition and visibility of their work. this requires the availability of statistical programmes specific to the regions concerned, which not only clearly define their work but also break down by sex indicators such as the age, educational level, education or activity of their spouses or partners, in order to have a good basis for subsequent policy-making. it is also important to ask for social, political and economic justice for all those women in the sector who have been working without any recognition, not even in the field of health and social security. it is also urgent to regulate and recognise as occupational diseases injuries to joints or the spine or rheumatic diseases caused by the harsh weather conditions in which shellfish-catching, packing, packaging, processing, processing, fishing and marketing women have to work, as well as those resulting from excessive weight lifting. we must not forget the need to encourage and financially support - as has also been said - the association of these women through networks which, at national or european level, are the object of our attention. it is important to raise the profile of the role played by these women in the sector and to raise awareness in society of the contribution these organisations and women make in relation to the common good and service. finally, it is also necessary to encourage and assist these organisations so that they can ensure greater parity in the decision-making bodies which are in operation at that time.
mr president, as chairman of the committee on fisheries, i have asked for the floor to congratulate the rapporteurs, mrs garcia-hierro and mr raül romeva, and to express my satisfaction that we have been able to reflect - even a little - on the reality of women in the fishing industry, who are so often forgotten. it is certainly inconceivable to talk about the fisheries sector without directly addressing the role of women and fishermen's families - who are also often overlooked. we have been able to reform the common fisheries policy, which i think is satisfactory; we have all been able to make concessions to win the whole thing, but in any case we will aim to have better and more sustainable fisheries, but we will only be able to do so if we value the role that women play in this activity.
mr president, today i bring to you the voice of the saltpeter women, of those who sew nets, who unload and sort fish, who supply ships: they are the rowers, the boatswainers and the packers, who do a job - hitherto invisible - that has never been recognised in european programmes or in the legislation of the member states. they're simple people, like my mother, who have spent their lives working while praying that the sea would return their family complete. meanwhile, they live off us by taking care of the house, by working in jobs that require complex apprenticeships, jobs with erratic and irregular hours, hard but essential. they are the rearguard of the fleet, of our basque fishing fleet. that's why i ask for justice for them and sensitivity. they support the report which recognises their work, as approved by the committee on fisheries.

in writing. - in favour. the european arrest warrant framework decision (henceforth ‘eaw fd’) approved in 2002 entered into operation on 1 january 2004 and is the most important eu legal instrument based on the mutual recognition principle whereby judicial decisions are executed on the basis of mutual trust. the objective of the eaw fd was to make it quicker and easier to bring suspects and accused persons to justice by transforming the old cumbersome extradition procedure involving politicians into a new faster surrender system through communication between judicial authorities. the eaw facilitates surrender by, inter alia, setting strict time limits and limiting the use of dual criminality as a ground for refusal. it requires the requested member state to execute the warrant without any assessment of the substance of the accusation or conviction.

member of the commission. - mr president, honourable members, mr silvestris, i must admit something. i think that that our communication strategy on this proposal has failed. because, if one were to look at the content of this directive, it is exactly the opposite of what it is being criticised for. for instance, the idea that traditional seeds will now be regulated gives the impression that they are not regulated today but that they will be. on the contrary, today they are being regulated, and with the new proposal they will have a lighter registration procedure. the same applies to fees. today member states can impose any fees, but with this proposal, smes are exempted from fees. this does not mean that the commission will not do its very best to engage itself with the co-legislators on some concerns which have been raised, but basically we believe the proposal is a good one, which had received considerable attention even before its launch in may[nbsp ]2013. first of all, let me clarify certain key issues. this proposal seeks to regulate the marketing of seeds. it does not seek to regulate their use, so all these criticisms that we are regulating the use of seed, whether on farms or in private gardens, are just not true. again, it does not seek to regulate intellectual protection of varieties or gmos, nor plant breeding as such or the size of companies in europe. this proposal also does not regulate the use of seed by private gardeners. private gardeners may buy, sell or produce material in small quantities without any testing and can exchange seeds with other private gardeners without falling under the rules of the proposed regulation. this was another main thrust of the criticism against this directive. so the aim of this proposal is simply to ensure the identity, health and quality of seed sold to users – be they farmers, gardeners, foresters or consumers. as you will appreciate, seed is an important economic factor for farmers and therefore also for agricultural and food production in the european union, and i would point out that european farming organisations – both organic and non-organic – support the revision of the legislation, as do seed suppliers and plant breeders, as well as the majority of member states. after 40 years, and with 12 separate directives in place, the evaluation of the current legislation showed a clear need to update, streamline and revise our legislation. first, on administrative burdens: these will be lessened with this directive, not increased. procedures are not going to become more complicated; they are going to become simpler. second, the aim of the directive is to introduce flexibility, where under the current legislation there is no flexibility, and to foster innovation and respond to the needs of specific types of production, whether conventional, traditional or organic. the third aim is to encourage innovation, with faster market access for new improved varieties and through sustainability criteria for variety testing. we believe the new concepts of plant reproductive material should lead to the creation of new business opportunities. the fourth aim – and in contrast to what is often claimed – the new proposal leads to lower administrative burdens and lower costs, especially for micro-enterprises. finally, as i said in the beginning, traditional varieties and new concepts of plant reproductive material, such as heterogeneous material and niche market material, would benefit from a significantly simplified path of access to the market – this would not, as is alleged, strangle these traditional varieties – and this will contribute to the conservation and sustainable use of plant genetic resources. let me highlight especially the issue of traditional varieties. for these varieties, market access has been made considerably easier, thus developing a much lighter regime in terms of both administrative burden and cost than is currently the case. at present – and some members conveniently forget this – even traditional varieties have to be tested, officially or using results provided by the applicant, for distinctness, stability and relative uniformity, and there are quantitative and areal marketing restrictions as the law stands today. according to our proposal – if it is approved – in order to register a traditional variety there will no longer be a requirement for any testing; all the applicant has to do is to provide a description which is recognised by the competent authority. secondly, quantitative and areal marketing restrictions have been abolished and, since testing is no longer required, registration fees are expected to fall. finally, all micro-enterprises – unlike the position today – will in any case be exempted from registration fees. so how can one criticise this directive by saying, with regard to traditional varieties, that it is making life harder? it is making life simpler. let me now come to another issue: the number of delegated acts. i appreciate that, each time we mention delegated acts, there is criticism from the european parliament. but may i remind this assembly that, with the current directive – if this is approved – the empowerments for secondary acts scattered in 12 different directives, amounting to 278, will – with the new directive – be reduced to 62: practically a 75[nbsp ]% decrease in the enabling acts of delegated acts. and the number of secondary acts themselves will be reduced from around 80 to fewer than 40. so, we can say – contrary to certain claims – that the proposal contains more substantial provisions than the existing 12 directives and therefore implies an increased involvement of parliament compared to the current situation. having explained all these points – and of course i defend the directive in so much as members of parliament criticise it – i can, however, assure you that i understand these concerns. i understand some of them; others i do not understand, and i would like to understand them. i understand the concerns regarding the highly technical nature of the proposal (but this is a technical matter), the high number of tabled amendments (i recognise that), and the short time available to examine the proposal. so i can also assure this assembly that the commission is willing to study the concerns as expressed in the tabled amendments, to look at the issue of delegated acts – even though we have made a reduction of almost 75[nbsp ]% – and to contribute to finding clarifications and solutions which take the interests of stakeholders into account, which is in the interest of this parliament and of the commission, and to find common ground to further improve this important proposal.
the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. - mr president, mr commissioner, i am very sorry that we have had to reject this proposal after the excellent work of mr silvestris in unifying these 12 directives into one regulation. you are right, commissioner, about the criticism of 'copy and paste' that has been levelled at this proposal. he didn't really deserve them. but it is not easy to include such different sectors within the same rule, and we think that this requires more rest and debate than can be had at the end of a legislature and at the end of a term of office of a college of commissioners. for example, the inclusion of forest reproductive material is not understood when it has nothing to do with food safety, which is one of the main arguments used by the commission in presenting this proposal. the proposal is too general in that it seeks to cover so many sectors in one technical standard. it also proposes vague definitions, giving rise to wide margins of interpretation, which would result in a huge administrative burden and legal uncertainty for member states and producers. this explains the huge number of delegated acts - many of which are unjustified - that are planned and that make future repercussions unpredictable. finally, i would like to say... member of the commission. - mr[nbsp ]president, the commission firmly believes that improvement of the negotiating position for small farmers requires an increased degree of organisation in the sector. fortunately, the available data show a steady increase in organisation, albeit at differing degrees in different member states. the reformed common market organisation regulation confirms and improves the provisions on producer organisations and associations in the fruit and vegetable sector. following the cap reform, the commission has started drafting the requisite delegated and implementing acts, and the input of parliament and the member states will be taken into account. these discussions will take place in the current year. the same will happen in relation to marketing standards, with further simplification where possible. the commission will present a report on producer organisations, operational funds and operational programmes in the fruit and vegetable sectors in the first quarter of this year. the conclusions of that report will be taken into account in the ongoing discussion on delegated and implementing acts. the commission has noted the call to create two different approval processes for cisgenic and transgenic plants. the commission has undertaken an analysis to clarify the legal status of the new breeding techniques under the current gmo legislation. the commission proposal for a regulation on plant reproductive material includes a number of provisions, such as fee exemptions and support for microenterprises, which are particularly relevant in the fruit and ornamentals sector. in addition, the proposal facilitates access to the market for traditional varieties and allows the marketing of heterogeneous material which contributes to genetic diversity within crop species. concerning organisms harmful to plants and plant products, the commission emphasises that the current eu legislation already ensures that import requirements for third countries closely mirror the requirements for intra-eu trade. the report also mentions the approval system for pesticides. here the commission acknowledges that we have one of the strictest procedures in the world. the overriding purpose is to ensure a high level of protection of human and animal health and the environment. the commission recognises that this may have an effect on the availability of plant protection products for eu farmers, and thus possibly on competitiveness. to address this problem, the commission has just adopted a report on the establishment of a fund for minor users, which will in particular benefit the fruit and vegetable sectors. furthermore, the commission, with member states, will support a research coordination network – era-net – on integrated pest management, with specific reference to minor users. this will contribute to the further development of integrated pest management, including non-chemical alternatives. the report also addresses food waste. this issue is gathering a lot of political support – and rightly so – as people are shocked to learn that we waste 30-50[nbsp ]% of the food we produce. this means we are wasting land, nitrates, water and energy and many other key resources used in food production. the commission will present a communication on sustainable food by this summer. the communication will set out a number of areas for action, with food waste as a central theme. we are also looking at how we can support member states in developing strategies to prevent food waste. a few examples of action are: offering clearer technical definitions of food waste, establishing an agreed methodology for collecting food-waste data, and setting targets for food-waste prevention as part of the revision of the waste framework directive. another avenue of action is the establishment of a working group with stakeholders to establish the best possible support measures at eu level. one of the issues concerns the possible role of short food-supply chains in mitigating the loss and waste of fruit and vegetables. eu food hygiene legislation also includes derogations for small farms and short food-supply chains. this facilitates direct consumer access to agricultural produce whilst ensuring consumer safety.
