the next item is the joint debate on:- the report by christel schaldemose, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the safety of consumer products and repealing council directive 87/357/eec and council directive 2001/95/ec (com (2013) 0078 - c7-0042/2013 - 2013/0049 (cod)) (a7-0355/2013),- the report by sirpa pietikäinen, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on product market surveillance and amending council directives 89/686/eec and 93/15/eec, 94/9/ec, 94/25/ec, 95/16/ec, 97/23/ec, 1999/23/ec, 2000/5/ec, 2000/5/ec, 2001/14/ec and 2001/14/ec (com (2013) 0078 - c7-0042/2013 - 2013/0049 (cod)) (a7-0355/2013),- the report by josef pietikäinen, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the european parliament and of the council on the internal market and consumer in consumer protection of consumer products and consumer products and consumer services, no 2003/1037/14/ec, no.
the package of legislation on consumer product safety is a major step forward in protecting european consumers and in boosting the competitiveness of our companies on international markets. i would like to focus my remarks on what i consider to be a vital step forward in this legislative package: the inclusion of mandatory origin labelling, detailed in article 7 of the regulation on the safety of consumer products. i think that this is a great opportunity for manufacturers, importers, consumers and, in particular, for our smes. for european smes, the commission has published a communication on the this measure creates a single, simpler standard for all and offers our companies, especially our smes, better access to and equal competition in the global market. in europe we manufacture our products to the highest quality standards in the world. we ask our companies to do more than our competitors ask of theirs. we must capitalise on our quality assurance. we must take advantage of the greater added value of our products. origin labelling also increases information to consumers, enabling them to make informed and conscious choices when consuming. the consumer must know where the products he buys come from, and he must be assured that they meet our high regulatory standards of quality and safety and that they are in line with our social, labour and environmental legislation, thus preventing abuse and allowing a better fight against counterfeiting. with 'made in', we filled a gap in european union legislation and created more of a european single market, more of a europe to get out of the crisis. it is not a protectionist measure, but rather the opposite: a europeanist measure. i therefore think it is essential to ask this house to support the adoption of this important article 7 of the regulation on the safety of consumer products.
mr president, this morning we are talking about costs or safety - both are compatible - and about product and market surveillance, which is necessary to ensure transposition and thus strengthen the confidence and security of citizens. but we must go further, and the council should know this, because with the improvement of the early warning system for dangerous products, their number has increased. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. in addition, as stated in article 7, the mandatory indication of the country of origin - true and essential information for consumers - and the traceability of products will make it possible to combat unfair competition and insecurity. i therefore welcome the adoption of this necessary measure because it has been supported by a large majority of the industrial sector. and we also need to pay attention to vulnerable consumers when assessing safety. finally, i congratulate my colleagues on the excellent work they have done and i encourage and call on the governments and the council to reach agreement as soon as possible and to transpose this important and decisive legislation in a timely manner.
member of the commission. - mr president, i would like once again to thank the honourable members, especially the rapporteurs ms[nbsp ]schaldemose and ms[nbsp ]pietikäinen, as well as the shadow rapporteurs, for the overall support they have shown for the commission’s proposal. today’s vote is an important milestone and sends out a strong signal that eu legislation can reconcile a high level of consumer safety, regulatory simplification for businesses, and effective enforcement by authorities. i hope that legislative negotiations will be launched soon to allow us to discuss outstanding issues, including certain amendments which we will need to address. i call therefore on the council to enter into negotiations with the european parliament and the commission on these two important legislative proposals as soon as possible. finally, sincere thanks to mr[nbsp ]weidenholzer for the utilities service report.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, a brief word to emphasize that article 7 is not intended to add to the burden of bureaucracy on businesses, but to send a strong signal in the fight against counterfeiting. the counterfeit represents a large market, equal to that of the drug trade, run by the criminal world. everything we do against it can only be positive. counterfeiting is damaging our health, our businesses and our jobs. i think it is therefore important to continue to support article 7, which is already used in many countries and by many producers, because it does not lead to bureaucratic or economic burdens, but protects workers, businesses and the health of our citizens.

in writing. - the three-part report on the banking union raises doubts as to the intergovernmental nature of its conception and is the second time that strategic economic and financial rules have been drawn up on the basis of an intergovernmental agreement. there has been significant progress, but the fact that so-called 'systemic' financial institutions will be able to continue operating in their current form leaves taxpayers still exposed to the losses generated by their speculative activities. to give visibility to these doubts, i have abstained in this report.
in writing. - one of the real and very important objectives within and for the european union is the establishment of an effective, and of course efficient, banking union. these proposals will legislate the fact of having a single bank resolution mechanism, thus sharing a single fund of almost 55 billion with the member states, to which the banks themselves will contribute, and which will be available in eight years at the latest. the commission has also proposed a rescue and resolution directive, which would require shareholders and creditors of banks to be the first to deal with potential losses of banks should any problems arise. in addition, the deposit guarantee will oblige banks to finance national funds up to eur 100,000, starting to apply from may 2015. the whole procedure will allow for an agile and efficient system in the management of banking institutions and, above all, will avoid taxpayers having to bear the costs of another bank rescue.
in writing. - the importance of small investors as citizens taking on risky activities in order to secure savings and financial security for themselves and their families must be the subject of an express guarantee that incorrect or insufficiently clear information will not lead to an unforeseen loss. it should be understood that we are talking about non-professional investors who need to have all the information necessary to clearly understand what they are doing, outside and outside of commercial or similar promotions, also knowing what final objectives may be behind the financial products mentioned. the requirements of civil liability which might be invoked in the event of a case being brought would be perfectly determined in the terms here approved.
in writing. - the ecall service is based on the installation of equipment approved for the single european emergency number 112 in all vehicles from certain categories, as well as the establishment of a framework for the management of ecall calls in telecommunications networks. this line will make ecall accessible to all citizens in europe, consolidating it as an eu-wide service, accelerating deployment and unlocking the full potential of the ecall system to save lives and reduce the severity of injuries. in parallel with this system, it is envisaged that other means or services of added value may be added, providing both economic and safety benefits.
in writing. - in the economic circumstances of the european union, it is necessary to improve the value of community products in order to cope more effectively with the globalisation of trade, to increase market shares both within and outside the european union and to react to critical situations. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment against the adverse effects of ionizing radiation is a very good one. the report also advocates a work programme which should provide a specific regime to react in the event of serious market disturbances or loss of consumer confidence. in designing this programme, the commission will have to take account of the handicaps of mountain areas, islands and the outermost regions.
in writing. - european agri-food products need to be promoted not only within the community's borders but also worldwide, thus providing support for expanding markets and opening up new opportunities. certain products will be given special aid, such as wine, but beer, chocolate, bread, pastries, pasta, salt, sweet corn and cotton will also be eligible for promotion. but not all those involved in fisheries and aquaculture will be left out. in this way, a sector as strategic as the agri-food sector is being helped to emerge from this general crisis, while at the same time promoting and fostering consumer confidence in european products. the contribution to these campaigns will be made not by the member states but by the european union's own funds and by the organisation responsible for each product.
in writing. - with the projected increase in the population aged 65 to 80 (by 40% between 2010 and 2030), finding solutions for active and healthy ageing and tackling demographic change is an urgent and pressing challenge in 21st century europe. on the other hand, the 'green' economy also provides an opportunity to develop innovative products and services that respond to social needs while driving economic growth and new business models. in the european research area, a number of initiatives have emerged to respond to the challenge of 'active and healthy ageing'. one of the main ones is the 'aided and active daily living' programme. this programme advocates the improvement of the quality of life of older citizens based on their increased use of new information and communication technologies.
in writing. - building on the success of the previous eureka programme, the report proposes eu participation in the eureka eurostars 2 programme, which promotes market-oriented research activities carried out by smes. the new financial contribution will be increased from eur 100 million to eur 287 million under the 'industrial leadership' section of horizon 2020.
in writing. - metrology is a fundamental element of our high-tech world. the overall objective of empir is to provide metrology solutions that support innovation and industrial competitiveness, as well as measurement technologies that address societal challenges such as health, environment and energy, including support for policy development and implementation. one of the important objectives of the proposal is the creation of an integrated european metrology research system with critical mass and active engagement at regional, national, european and international levels. the programme, which started in 2014, was co-funded by the european union and the participating countries. the proposal is to continue until 2020 with a budget of 300 million euros, compared with the original 200 million.
in writing. - the proposal will require certain large companies to include a statement in their annual report on information relating to at least environmental, social and employee-related issues, respect for human rights and anti-corruption and bribery issues. the obligation will only apply to those enterprises in which the average number of employees is more than 500 and to their subsidiaries. i regret that a mention of disability has not been included among the statements that the company must make in its annual report, as the prestigious spanish organization once demands and as i have tried unsuccessfully in the development of this report. it is essential that disability is addressed, otherwise it will continue to cause discrimination and social exclusion to the detriment of all.
in writing. - there is scope for developing sustainable bio-based industries in europe. however safeguards to ensure these are environmentally sound, do not lead to negative effects such as land-use change, land grabbing, competition with food production or downgrading of the use of biomass are not sufficiently provided for in the proposed joint undertaking. so, i abstained.
in writing. - i voted against because i think the report is too favourable to large companies in the sector and, for example, does not contain any conditions for access to employment creation funds in europe. small companies in the sector will also be disadvantaged in accessing r & d funds and will probably have to act as subcontractors for large companies.
in writing. - i voted against the amendments to respect the interinstitutional agreement adopted, but i support their content, particularly as regards the improvement of the transparency of the operation of the joint undertakings.
- the tripartite social summit for growth and employment was established on the basis of the council decision of 6 march 2003 to institutionalize informal high-level meetings. its task is to ensure continuous cooperation between the council, the commission and the social partners, in accordance with the treaty and taking into account the competences of the union institutions and bodies. the report proposes to extend the tasks of the social summit to include the coordination of the parties' strategies for growth, high employment, social integration, education, training and health protection. it also states that the outcome of the summit should be presented to the european council for decision-making.
member of the commission. - madam president, i believe the discussion has confirmed the importance of this directive. it helps to foster the mobility of workers. it helps to improve working conditions in europe and also helps the better functioning of the single market. that is why the proposal was also included in the single market act. i think it has been confirmed that this is a balanced proposal which offers tangible improvements to european workers, without putting an excessive burden on pension funds or employers. as the commission outlined in its white paper on pensions, promoting safe supplementary pensions is highly instrumental in sustaining adequate pensions against the background of ageing populations and increasing labour mobility in europe. ageing is indeed a common european challenge, but the eu is not taking decisions instead of the member states concerning the design of pension systems within the member states. i believe the white paper clarified the common objective of pension systems to have adequate, safe and sustainable pensions in all eu member states. which specific combination of the various pillars satisfies these goals remains within the competence of the member states in the eu. ensuring the preservation of occupational and pension rights of mobile workers will become increasingly important in a context where an important part of the working population relies at least partially on supplementary pension provisions, due to national and also individual decisions. that is why this debate has been so important and that is why i personally also appreciate so much the work of the rapporteur, ria oomen-ruijten. congratulations.

agreement on the directive on the posting of workers. this agreement was confirmed at coreper on 5 march and by the european parliament's committee on employment and social affairs on 18 march. the agreement reached is a balanced text. this is welcome in itself, given the very different positions of our two institutions at the start of the negotiations. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. we have managed to reach agreement on a directive which, from the point of view of cross-border application, contains a significant number of extensive and innovative elements. i think we can all be very pleased with the result. in these negotiations, the role of the european commission is often crucial. and that is certainly true in this particular case and i would like to thank commissioner andor here. at critical moments, the commission was the key to helping the two co-legislators to find a compromise solution. the agreement was, however, largely possible because of the determination and commitment of the two co-legislators. i believe that each of us negotiated in a constructive way, listened carefully to the other's concerns and made no effort to make the final result - the directive - transparent and effective. that's vital in these kinds of negotiations. i would like to congratulate the negotiating team of the european parliament, in particular the rapporteur, mrs danuta jazłowiecka, and the chairman of the committee on employment and social affairs, mrs pervenche berès. both worked hard to keep all the groups at the negotiating table when we were trying to bridge important differences. with this common will to succeed, we have been able to find solutions to complex issues. in particular, the text now covers parliament's concerns regarding undeclared work, the reference to the rome i regulation and sham self-employment. it also takes into account the council's concerns regarding national control measures and joint and several liability. i also believe that it has fulfilled a key objective which was to improve and strengthen the way in which this directive is applied in practice throughout the union. this directive is important for the approximately one million workers who are posted by their employers each year from their country of origin to another country to carry out temporary work. the work carried out by these people is essential for the provision of crossborder services in a number of areas. it is particularly important for those service activities which require a skilled and trained workforce. at the same time, labour mobility and economic freedom must not be used to achieve a 'downward equalization' of working conditions. this means that the right balance had to be struck between protecting workers' rights and facilitating the exercise of economic freedom, including cross-border activities. this agreement fully addresses this challenge by establishing a general common framework of appropriate measures, including measures to prevent any circumvention of rights or breach of rules. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented in a uniform manner. this should now facilitate the renewal of trust between national authorities, workers and businesses. it is an important achievement in the strengthening of social europe. i am convinced that the implementation of these provisions will help to facilitate the free provision of services and to safeguard the rights to which posted workers are entitled and which they should expect to be respected. thank you very much.
member of the commission. - madam president, let me start by thanking the rapporteur, ms danuta jazłowiecka, and the chair of the committee on employment and social affairs, ms pervenche berès, as well as the negotiating team, for having spared no efforts to find acceptable compromise solutions despite divergent points of departure between the co-legislators on this proposal. i also thank the greek presidency for working so hard for a good result. over twelve trialogues were held in a very short period of time. discussions were difficult until the last moment, but both institutions demonstrated the necessary spirit of flexibility which finally paved the way for reaching an agreement on the text as a whole. the compromise text is a balanced one. it contains a comprehensive package of appropriate measures for better enforcement and implementation of the rules governing the posting of workers. it guarantees better protection of posted workers and companies involved, as well as setting out a more transparent and predictable legal framework for service providers in the single market. parliament has insisted on a number of points which have been taken on board and which the commission considers to be helpful. for example: the introduction of the criteria to be used for classification as a worker by the host member state; the reference to bogus self-employment; and the need to protect non-genuine posted workers in line with regulation (ec) no 593/2008 of the european parliament and of the council of 17 june 2008 on the law applicable to contractual obligations (rome i). as regards control measures, the compromise text acknowledges member states’ competencies to implement such measures while guaranteeing increased transparency for service providers and providing for an ex-post monitoring mechanism by the commission. in addition, specific concerns as regards the role of the social partners have been taken up in the compromise text. furthermore, and to a large extent following the commission proposal, the compromise text greatly improves the protection of workers’ rights in sub-contracting chains – in particular in the construction sector. it introduces the possibility for workers to hold the contractor in a direct sub-contractor relationship liable for any outstanding net remuneration corresponding to the minimum rates of pay in addition to, or in place of, their employer. besides these key provisions, the text also provides for increased cooperation between all administrations involved, improved access to information, and the cross-border enforcement of fines and penalties. altogether, the comprehensive package of measures will considerably improve the current situation and provide for a number of appropriate tools to improve the protection of posted workers’ rights and prevent social dumping. considering the provisionally agreed text as the best compromise that could be reached, the time has now come to close the deal.
madam president, i would first of all like to thank the rapporteur for the work she has done for so long with the other members, and i ask that the agreement reached, an agreement which will affect one million workers, be voted in favour. despite differences between member states and political groups, a good balance has been struck between the provision of services and the protection of posted workers, improving the current situation and thus moving towards a european labour market. in times of economic and employment crisis and difficulties, mobility must become one of the key tools to combat them, and the displacement of workers must be a safe way of working across national borders that respects workers' rights and fights against so-called 'false displaced persons'. cooperation and mutual assistance between member states is therefore one of the most important achievements, as it will facilitate the implementation of controls and inspections, help to detect and investigate abuses and infringements of the applicable rules and, above all, allow cross-border enforcement of the sanctions imposed, something which was not possible today. the text will also facilitate the implementation, application and enforcement of the posting of workers directive and improve access to information on host country working conditions and applicable collective agreements through the single national website. in short, the aim of this directive is to protect workers, regardless of the member state in which they are employed. finally, i would like to emphasize the possibility for the member states to take the control measures they consider appropriate, within the framework of article 9, to ensure compliance with the obligations laid down.

the next item on the agenda is the debate on the statement by the vice-president of the commission and high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy on russian pressure on the eastern partnership countries and in particular the destabilisation of eastern ukraine (2014/2699 ((rsp)).
member of the commission, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. - mr president, honourable members, it was mid-december when we discussed the outcome of the vilnius summit and the massive support for reform, modernisation and a chance to live by european values shown by ukrainian citizens in the streets and squares of kiev and other ukrainian cities. we then concluded that in our eastern partnership we respect and defend the rights and freedoms of each individual, and we must defend the right of every nation to make its own choices. a couple of months ago, we reiterated that russia – the neighbour of our neighbour – can only gain from ukraine’s success and it therefore has a chance to become a part of the joint efforts to bring stability and prosperity back to ukraine. yet, the latest developments in ukraine show that the notion of europe, whole and free, based on shared commitments to human rights and freedoms, democracy and the rule of law, as well as the freedom and sovereignty of all the european states, their right to choose their own destiny and their freedom of association, is being challenged in an extremely serious and dangerous way. the coordinated and professional actions by the armed groups, including those penetrating into ukrainian territory from abroad, in eastern ukraine, resemble the crimea scenario. the european union has appealed to the russian federation to call back its troops from the ukrainian border and cease any further actions aimed at destabilising ukraine. any threat or use of force – be it military force or economic coercion – against ukraine or any other countries is not acceptable and must be stopped. it is in our common interest to avoid violence and bloodshed on the european continent which could spiral out of control. it is in our common interest to jointly work towards the establishment of a common area of prosperity, stability and democracy on the european continent. yet, such an area can only be established on the basis of the helsinki osce principles and in line with international law. developments in the upcoming days will demonstrate the choice of russia. but they may also require unequivocal choices on our side. our responses to the crisis in ukraine-russia relations, as well as our efforts to bring stability, security and prosperity back to ukraine, are comprehensive. firstly, on diplomatic efforts: quadrilateral talks on ukraine that are taking place tomorrow have been the european union’s preferred framework and come at our initiative as well. the european union has been firm in insisting that any solution on ukraine must be peaceful, must involve ukraine and must be based on full respect for ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, including the right of ukraine to decide on its own constitution and political future. the high representative and vice-president, catherine ashton, has been very closely engaged, leading these efforts on the european union side. she will meet the foreign ministers of the united states, the russian federation and ukraine in geneva tomorrow, in an attempt to de-escalate the crisis and to engage russia in a forward-looking process. given the complex situation in ukraine, it is a considerable success that these international talks are taking place. the eu has also strongly supported the establishment of an osce special monitoring commission. it is doing very valuable work on the ground in the eastern regions. the european union has provided and will continue providing actual substantial assistance to the mission, to ensure that it can carry out its mandate in the best way possible. furthermore, at the last foreign affairs council, an important step was also taken towards a possible csdp mission. secondly, the european union has taken a firm and united stance after the illegal annexation of crimea by russia, including sanctions against individuals responsible for undermining the territorial integrity of ukraine. condemning the actions undertaken by armed individuals in cities of eastern ukraine, the european union has decided to further expand the list of those subject to asset freezes and visa bans. these measures can gradually be enlarged to a broad range of economic areas, should russia continue to destabilise ukraine. thirdly, the european union has not recognised the illegal annexation of crimea and is working to establish the practical parameters of this non-recognition policy. fourthly, the eu is firmly committed to providing strong political and financial backing to ukraine. on 21 march, we signed the political chapters of the association agreement and we have just adopted a set of unilateral trade measures that will open the european union’s door to exports from ukraine. we remain committed to concluding the signature procedure of the remaining chapters of the association agreement as soon as possible after the 25 may presidential elections. at the end of march i was in kiev with commissioner lewandowski and several directors-general of the commission to agree on a joint plan. we have moved fast on this, and last week the european commission created a support group which will help ukraine to implement this plan – a so-called european agenda for reform – which lists the political and economic reforms we agreed with ukraine, based on their needs. clear progress has been made already on the financial front: the foreign affairs council adopted on monday a decision on a eur 1 billion macro-financial assistance programme. another issue of critical importance is energy security. the letter by president putin to 18 member states and five partner countries illustrates well just how important this issue is. the european union will respond jointly to the letter, in order to agree on consultations with russia and ukraine, with a view to ensuring security of supply and transit. allow me to emphasise: our relations with russia on energy are those of mutual interdependence. the european union is the largest market for russian gas and oil. furthermore, in reaction to recent developments, the european commission will, as requested by the european council, conduct an in-depth study of eu energy security and will present a comprehensive plan for the reduction of european union energy dependence. we are committed to facilitating an agreement between the slovak and ukrainian gas operators on reverse flow. moreover, the ukrainian government is aware of the need to reform the energy sector in line with the energy community commitments, and displays determination to commence these reforms. while ukraine is naturally at the centre of our attention, we are likewise following the situation very closely in moldova and georgia. political developments in both countries need to be watched carefully as we prepare for the signature and implementation of association agreements including the deep and comprehensive free trade areas (dcftas), and given the existing external vulnerabilities. we are increasing our political engagement, including with high level visits by presidents van rompuy and barroso. the european commission has also invited the ukrainian, moldovan and georgian governments to brussels in may. we should note the unprecedented speed with which the procedures bringing the association agreements with moldova and georgia have been completed. the time has been cut by more than two thirds, enabling us to sign the agreements already in june. moreover, visa liberalisation with moldova will take effect in only a couple of days, on 28 april. this is a key achievement, bringing clear benefits to the entire population. in parallel, we encourage georgia and the republic of moldova to continue implementing reforms as part of their commitment to further strengthen their political association and economic integration with the european union.

in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it represents a step forward towards a regulation which will allow european consumers to have access to safe consumer products. the report proposes an amendment to the legislation requiring economic operators to comply with active control measures for any product placed on the eu market. this raises costs and increases the liability of economic operators for any risks to which consumers are exposed. the report extends the scope of this regulation to professional equipment, services, products sold through online sales, etc. all these changes to the rules will make it possible to operate a safer market and to introduce more controls to prevent abuse by companies. that is why i voted in favour of this report.

president-in-office of the council. - mr president, i would like first of all to thank both mr[nbsp ]lamassoure and ms[nbsp ]jensen for their very comprehensive presentation of this very important file and very important debate on own resources. i understand that the efforts of this parliament to change the own resources system has not yet given concrete results but i think the effort to have a more simple, transparent system of own resources will continue afterwards with the next parliament and the next commission. as you all know there was a proposal which was presented by the commission in 2011 which was linked to the multiannual financial framework (mff) for the period 2014-2020. these proposals were examined by the council and the preparatory bodies of the council, in parallel with the mff and an agreement was reached at the european council meeting in february 2013 covering not only the expenditure side of the mff, but also its financing – the revenue side. it then took a few more months until the two institutions, parliament and the council, agreed on a common understanding of all elements related to the mff package: the new mff regulation, the new interinstitutional agreement, the different sectoral legislative proposals, and also a number of joint statements. one of these statements related to the very important issue of own resources and it acknowledged that further work is needed on this question. it was therefore agreed to create a high-level group on own resources which has recently started its work. the council welcomes the recent start of the work of this group and we are convinced that the group, under the chairmanship of mr[nbsp ]monti, will carry out excellent work. we fully support the work of the group and look forward with interest to the first assessment which should be available at the end of this year. over the next two years the group will undertake a general review of the own resources system which is, as it has already been said, very complex. on that basis the commission will assess whether new own resource initiatives are appropriate, which could then be taken into consideration by the commission when it prepares its proposals for the next multiannual financial framework. for the period 2014-2020, the council reached an agreement on a package of three legislative proposals in order to bring the system of own resources in line with the provisions of the lisbon treaty and the new mff. the council agreed to establish a regulation laying down implementing measures on the system of own resources, as foreseen in article[nbsp ]311 of the treaty, and it agreed on a limited number of modifications to the two existing elements of the own resources: the council decision on the system of own resources, and the council regulation on the methods and procedure for making available own resources and to meet cash requirements. the agreement reached in the council takes into account the conclusions of the european council of february 2013. they provide that the system of own resources of the european union will remain mainly unchanged for the period 2014-2020, with the exception of some modifications to the correction mechanisms in favour of certain member states, and a reduction in the share of costs retained by member states for the collection of traditional own resources. now it is parliamentʼs turn, as laid down in the treaty. parliament has been invited to consider the legislative package agreed by the council, and it has been asked to give its consent to the draft council regulation laying down implementing measures on the system of own resources – the new element which has been introduced by the treaty of lisbon. i would especially like to thank parliamentʼs rapporteurs, ms[nbsp ]jensen and mr[nbsp ]dehaene – whom i would also like to wish an early recovery – and mr[nbsp ]lamassoure for their professionalism and for their constructive approach during this last period which has made it possible to have this debate today. i very much look forward to this parliamentʼs adoption of the opinion and its consent to these various files so that they can be closed before the end of the current legislature. this would pave the way for the process of national ratification as is provided for in the treaty.

the next item is the report by rosa estaràs ferragut, on behalf of the committee on regional development, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending council regulation (ec) no 2012/2002 establishing the european union solidarity fund (com (2013) 0522 - c7-0231/2013 - 2013/0248 (cod)) (a7-0078/2014).
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. you know that this is a fund which was set up in 2002 and is the most visible symbol of solidarity when a natural disaster strikes a member state, or even those states which are negotiating accession. before 2002 there was no instrument to mitigate the damage caused by a disaster, and after its entry into force, now 12 years ago, we were able to determine, on behalf of all the sectors, that it was an instrument that could be improved because during its period of validity it had had problems in its application, especially with regard to the agility and simplification of the fund and with regard to the possible expectations on the part of some regions about whether or not to access this fund. in 2005, the commission - and also parliament - tried unsuccessfully to amend the fund - precisely to achieve the fund's objectives of simplification and efficiency - but it was not well received and was eventually shelved. it is now, in 2014, that this change has been possible and has been undertaken almost unanimously. i hope that in the vote this afternoon the result will be as unanimous as possible. after a series of negotiations between the council, the commission and parliament itself, it has been substantially improved in several respects. you know that there was no problem with the issue of serious national natural disasters, it was very clear: anything up to 0.6% of gross national income was eligible for aid from the fund and an absolute amount. but where there were real problems was in regional disasters - which account for two thirds of this fund - because, until now, the regulation was very unclear, in the sense that it spoke of all those disasters which generate serious and lasting repercussions on living conditions and economic stability in the region. these concepts were very vague and we have therefore modified them to include all disasters which represent or exceed 1.5% of the gross domestic product of the region and, in the case of the outermost regions, 1%. this was a request from all the regions, because this way false expectations are not created and it will be known at the first minute when a region can submit the project or not. another issue that was also on the table was the issue of the fund's agility. advances were requested: in short, that the regions could collect at the moment of the catastrophe - this is very important: immediacy - a whole series of advances. and, after a whole series of technical hurdles, these advances have been made a reality: up to 30 million euros and 10% of the budget. another issue was the time-limits: there was a 10-week deadline for member states to present the project to the regions. these 10 weeks were short and the deadline has been extended to 12 weeks as a supplementary period so that the documentation needed in the supplementary period can be submitted. the deadline for justifying these funds has also been extended: up to now there was a deadline of 12 months, but it has been extended to 18 months - a year and a half - because this was also better for the regions, and a new deadline has been set: within six weeks, the commission has to answer to the member state or the region whether it will be able to receive this aid or not. finally, long-term disasters such as floods or droughts will also be covered by the fund, and the time limits will start to run from the last day of the disaster. and, in conclusion, i must say that the goodwill of all has been counted on. i think the fund will be greatly expanded and it is a great day because we believe it is the most visible image of solidarity. that is why we in this parliament have welcomed the adoption of the amendment to the fund after more than 12 years of operation.
member of the commission. - mr president, on behalf of my colleague johannes hahn who cannot be with us today, many thanks to the rapporteur ms[nbsp ]estaràs ferragut, and to the chair of the committee on regional development, ms[nbsp ]hübner. the compromise was reached and then unanimously adopted in the regional development committee which is a signal that this was quite a good deal. this is a final vote on a long procedure. the procedure considering how to amend the european union solidarity fund started with our proposal in 2005. however, in the reality of today’s europe, this was probably too ambitious a proposal but i can agree anyway that the solidarity fund is needed, is a must. it is making europe visible. since 2002 when the solidarity fund was born as a reaction to the floods in germany and austria, we have approved 56 applications, paying financial aid and financial compensation of eur[nbsp ]3.5 billion to 23 countries. but, on the other hand, experience says it was very slow to mobilise, provoking frustration. indeed emergency aid reserves, the mobilisation of money vis-à-vis countries beyond the european union, were quicker than mobilisation of the solidarity fund within the european union. corrections were needed therefore and there are some positive corrections as enumerated by the rapporteur: a 10% advance payment shortly after application by a member state; member of the commission. - mr president, on behalf of vice-president almunia i would like to thank mr schwab for the work he has done and also mr rapkay and the chair of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, ms bowles, as well as all the shadow rapporteurs and everybody who has been involved in this very important directive and the constructive approach that you have all had. following the very fruitful cooperation of all the three institutions, the commission believes that we have achieved a very satisfying result. we especially welcome that we can adopt this today at the very last moment before you all go campaigning. i would like to underline the importance of the directive. it has been described by the press as the most important development in competition policy of the last years and as a democratisation of the competition law enforcement. when vice-president almunia was before you in his hearing four years ago, he promised that parliament would be fully involved in this file as co-legislator. as a consequence, today we bring this file negotiated under the ordinary legislative procedure to a successful end. more than 10 years ago the court of justice first recognised that any victim of anti-trust infringement had a right to compensation. but that was difficult to achieve in practice. in recent years we have seen very few actions and many of them have failed because of inadequate legal frameworks. consumers and small companies, especially, have found it difficult to obtain compensation for the harm they suffered. this directive is thus of utmost importance. it enables citizens and businesses harmed by anti-trust infringements to effectively exercise the right to compensation that the eu is granting them. the directive includes rules that remove the current obstacles. it gives victims better access to the evidence they need to prove their claims and it ensures that victims can overcome the burden of providing a competition law infringement. one way to do this is by allowing victims to use the infringement decisions of competition authorities in their own claims. in parallel, the directive also clarifies the relationship between public and private enforcement of eu competition laws, in particular when it comes to accessing documents that are in the possession of a competition authority. the text that you will be voting tomorrow preserves a company’s incentives to cooperate with competition authorities through leniency programmes and settlement procedures. defending the effectiveness of competition authorities is good news for the victims of anti-trust infringements. the more decisions are taken, the easier it will be for the victims to claim damages. the commission believes that the text has reached an excellent balance. on the one hand, it will be easier for victims to exercise the right to compensation. on the other hand, it ensures the continued effectiveness of the public enforcement of competition law by europe’s competition authorities, and for this i wish to deeply thank you all.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, as rapporteur for the green paper on private actions for damages for infringements of competition law, i secured the adoption of a parliament resolution seven years ago, and having represented my group as rapporteur in all resolutions on the subject since then, i am pleased that we finally have a legislative initiative and that agreement has been reached in a three-way dialogue. i would like to congratulate mr schwab, mr rapkay and all the rapporteurs who have helped me to achieve this. the directive will strengthen the protection of the rights of european citizens and increase security in the internal market. it is a milestone in the union's competition policy - an integral part of the european union's dna since the treaty of rome - and makes it more effective, fairer and more democratic. more effective, because, alongside the pillar of public actions taken by the competent authorities, it places a pillar of private actions in the judicial field which will have a deterrent character incentivising compliance with the rules and a guaranteeing character ensuring that imbalances are restored in the event of non-compliance. more fair, because whereas the union's competition policy has so far focused on prosecuting offenders by putting an end to unlawful conduct and imposing penalties, it will now also be geared to protecting victims by ensuring that they obtain compensation for the damage suffered. it is also more democratic, since it is the first time that parliament has intervened as a legislator in an initiative aimed at the effectiveness of competition policy. this fulfils the commitment made by commissioner joaquín almunia to the committee on economic and monetary affairs during the hearing before his appointment. the democratic principle requires parliamentary intervention in those matters which are closely related to the right to judicial protection, especially in order to give effect to all the fundamental rights of european citizens. the directive promotes competition and not litigation. it seeks solutions that avoid excesses and uncertainties and always favours the extrajudicial settlement of disputes. the principle of the right to compensation is part of the recognised principle of the right to claim and obtain compensation, but at the same time it provides that the right to compensation does not imply overcompensation or recognition of punitive damages. the compromise reached ensures access to evidence and avoids overreach, ensuring that this power is not used inquisitively in an unjustified, arbitrary or indiscriminate manner. the public and private actions are articulated by providing for conditions of access to the files of the competition authorities, ensuring the value of the decisions of the competition authorities and providing that the payment of compensation resulting from an amicable settlement may be a mitigating factor in the setting of fines. the clemency programmes will not be undermined because clemency statements are protected under judicial control and, even if joint and several liability is provided for by the members of a cartel, there are special rules for clemency applicants and, under certain conditions, for small and medium-sized enterprises. balanced rules are established to address pass-on and the commission is mandated to prepare guidelines on how to estimate the pass-on share of cargo. finally, i would like to say that although the principles on class actions are not included - as we would have liked - to ensure public action in minor and diffuse damages, it is a positive initiative. this is my last speech after ten years in the european parliament. i would like to thank those who have given me the opportunity to work for the construction of europe during this time and those who have collaborated with me in this work. it has been a great satisfaction to be able to work towards building in europe an area of trust based on progress and solidarity.

president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, you have asked the council and the commission to make a statement on the state of payments in the budget of the european union. this is a matter directly linked to the budget negotiations under way this year. the council recognises that there is a specific problem with regard to invoices and late payments, particularly in the area of cohesion policies. these payments, like all others, must of course be made. the council's interest is obviously that no member state should have to face the consequences of a problem which is likely to lead to an increase in national budget deficits on its own. but there is another important aspect of the budget which concerns the way in which a proper balance is struck between two different orders of interests. on the one hand, we must respect the commitments we have made, and on the other hand we must take account of the need to ensure that the budget of the european union reflects the requirement that individual member states fully comply with the deficit targets set in the stability and growth pact, a requirement which is first and foremost a european obligation. it is true that last year we agreed annual budget ceilings from 2014 to 2020 in the multiannual financial framework, but these ceilings do not constitute spending targets. they should be assessed annually in the light of the economic situation of the member states and the possible impact on national budgets. this parliament, together with the council, adopted a package of legislation three years ago which lays down the basic rules which impose this budgetary discipline on the member states. the budget of the european union therefore requires careful planning. member states' requests to create sufficient margins below the ceilings are made in an attempt to control unforeseen or unexpected financial needs. i therefore strongly hope that we can avoid a debate in which the european union is divided into good and bad people, those who want to spend generously and those who want to save first and foremost. we're all in the same boat. we want to use and invest the eu budget in the most effective way to stimulate innovation, growth and jobs. at the same time, we must bear in mind the budgetary constraints within which we are operating. the experience of the last two years shows that the council is always ready to respond to proposals to cover justified and urgent payment needs. last year we approved an amending budget of eur 11.2 billion. why did we ask for it to be split in two? to ensure adequate control of changes in payment needs, but also to assist the national budgetary authorities in adjusting to the additional financial burden resulting from them. this year we will participate in the same spirit in the discussion and negotiations on the draft amending budgets which are on the table, as well as on the draft budget for 2015. although the backlog of payments in the cohesion sector was very high towards the end of last year, it has decreased significantly from eur 23 billion to eur 10 billion in the first half of this year. we are obviously going through a transition phase between the accumulated invoices at the end of a programming period and the start of a new period in which a certain amount of time is needed for the implementation of the programmes and for them to be fully effective in terms of leverage. we should take advantage of this situation rather than risk a failure of our negotiations. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, our national economies and the need to promote growth in investment require a european union budget designed and implemented in the most effective way to achieve results. the italian presidency is ready to devote all its energies to achieving this objective. thank you for your attention.
member of the commission. - mr president, the commission welcomes this discussion on the payments situation in the eu budget at the start of the parliament’s new term. the discussion is indeed timely, as both branches of the budgetary authority are engaging in discussions on the amending budgets for 2014, requesting additional payment appropriations, and on the 2015 draft budget. over the last few years, the budgetary authority has effectively followed a two-step approach whereby, first, an artificially low level of payment appropriations was authorised in the budget with the understanding, reflected in a recurrent joint statement, that a supplementary amending budget might be needed in the course of the year once implementation provided compelling evidence that more payment appropriations were needed. we saw this in 2012, when an amending budget of eur 6 billion was adopted at the end of the year, and again in 2013 when, thanks in particular to the determination and support of parliament, an additional eur 11.2 billion was eventually made available to cover outstanding needs. this approach in agreeing the budget in successive stages makes the budgetary process almost unintelligible and undermines the eu’s credibility. the eu budget should serve to implement our common priorities. this must be taken with seriousness and realism, addressing all the foreseen needs in the knowledge that the new multiannual financial framework (mff) provides the tools to address unforeseen needs should they arise. the commission proposals for the 2015 draft budget and for amending the 2014 budget reflect a responsible and realistic approach but again, realistically, they will only lead to stabilising the overall situation. the new mff provides for enhanced flexibility, not least thanks to the determination of parliament. the commission has consistently made it clear that the overall payment ceiling defined in the 2014-2020 mff would require the implementation of specific and maximum flexibility, and that it would make use of available flexibility instruments as provided for in the mff regulation if and where needed. this is what the commission did in late may this year by presenting draft amending budget no 3, with a request to use the remaining margin under the payment ceiling – some eur 700 million – and the activation of the contingency margin mechanism for an amount of eur 4 billion. such a request is justified by the payment shortages experienced in several programmes and by a number of unforeseen circumstances, including a higher than expected pace of implementation in cohesion policy, which led to an unprecedented level of unpaid bills at the end of 2013 to be covered with appropriations in the 2014 budget. for the 2015 draft budget, the commission proposes to make full use of the payment ceiling agreed in the multiannual financial framework. combined with a careful management of resources these measures should curb the global growth of outstanding commitments and provide the means to address our obligations stemming from previous years’ commitments. let me take this opportunity to give a face to this problem. it is not just about ministries or universities or even member states as such, getting money back later than expected. in many programmes, for example in research and innovation, we have small private companies that have valid contracts and have performed their agreed work and incurred the agreed costs and now could face a situation in which the commission simply cannot pay them in time. the commission will have to mitigate these risks. in this context, the risk of sme bankruptcy will be one important factor to consider. these proposals are also a key condition to kick-start the new investments in infrastructure, innovation, growth and jobs needed for the new period 2014-2020, precisely in line with the strategic priorities for the union as agreed by the heads of state and government on 26 and 27 june. developments on the revenue side should greatly facilitate the solution. exceptional additional revenue from fines stemming from the enforcement of competition policy will accrue on the eu budget in 2014, meaning that the additional payments requested for 2014 will be at virtually no cost to the member states. at the budgetary trilogue last week, parliament and the council had a first opportunity to exchange views on the commission proposals for the three amending budgets for 2014 and for the 2015 draft budget. the commission is doing everything within its powers to address a difficult situation. we can only hope that the council and parliament will soon reach agreement on a sustainable solution.
i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this. we have been dragging this problem along for several years, mainly because of the incomprehensible attitude which the member states have so far taken in the council. in 2010, we ended with €5.5 billion in unpaid bills; in 2011, with €11 billion; in 2012, we went up to €16 billion; and in 2013 we ended with €25 billion in unpaid bills. it is clear that this situation is unsustainable and if we do not remedy it now, we shall end up with a suspension of payments. it could appeal to legality and sound financial management, which requires that the european institutions make available the necessary resources so that the union can meet its legal obligations. it could appeal to the credibility of the european union and the need for our partners to trust that we will meet our international commitments; or to the fulfilment of the agreements of the european council, which, for example, at its last meeting agreed on the need to invest and prepare the economies of the member states to meet needs in transport, energy or telecommunications. but, frankly, these appeals have never been of any use. we have given them reasons and we have given them figures and the council has continued to act as usual: not paying and cutting money. i am glad to hear the council admit that we have a problem, but it has just agreed on the level of payments for 2015 and cut the european commission's proposal by 2 billion. honestly, i don't know what his plan is. i don't know if they have it. i do not know whether they think that by not addressing the problem we are going to solve it, and that is why i would like to hear from the italian presidency, which we are counting on to solve this problem, the proposal for a package of measures to put an end to the problem of non-payments. and i'm going to give you a few ideas. first, to approve the amending budgets, to reduce this debt by eur 4.7 billion. secondly, we must work on a revision of the financial framework in order to be able to raise these payment ceilings. thirdly, to give the high-level group a definitive boost and to work on new own resources for the european union project. fourthly, to draw up a proposal for financial instruments to enable resources to be mobilised in order to be able to invest in the long term in this investment plan which the union so badly needs. and fifth, for example, to draw up a proposal to exclude from the accounting of the deficit of the countries the national contribution to the european budget, and thus to ease the strains on national finances. we have given you reasons, figures and even solutions, but if you need more examples i will give them to you. because behind these unpaid bills are municipalities, there are small businesses that need their money back, and there are ngos too. i would like to end, mr president, with one last example: humanitarian aid programmes have been paralysed and 400 iraqi families have no money or food.

madam president, commissioner, i regret that my first speech in this parliament is to denounce the damage being done to the agricultural and livestock sector as a result of the embargo imposed by the russian government. i think the european union should act more responsibly, considering that this is a very serious matter whose causes are completely outside the sector. emergency aid should be directed to those who are really affected by this crisis, extended to the sectors that are needed - as, for example, now citrus - and taking into account the cascading effect of some producers on others - and i am referring, for example, to mushrooms. it is common knowledge that the current suspension of aid is due to certain abuses detected in some member states in the aid application process. this suspension has been met with great concern by the producers, who need to see clearly the support of the union in this context, and i would therefore ask you, commissioner, to comply with what has been announced and to present a system for the distribution of emergency aid on 16 september which does not lead to unbalanced situations. the european commission should, in my view, be seriously considering the possibility of taking a new action against russia before the world trade organisation, and as regards the question of economic resources, the funds should not be confined to the agricultural budget but should also come from other chapters of the union budget, bearing in mind that, as we have said, this is a problem generated by circumstances totally outside the sector.
madam president, the russian embargo on european products is not only having serious effects on our farmers and livestock farmers, with particular impact on more fragile regions such as the canary islands, but also on the fisheries and aquaculture sector, which is being seriously affected. i have to admit that i would have liked to see the same diligence as commissioner cioloș in these sectors, because we must not forget that exports of fishery products to russia account for 5% of the european union's total. in fact, russia is our sixth largest market. that is why i would like to draw the commission's attention from here today to farmers, but also to our fishermen, so that it takes account of and acts on the possible consequences of this crisis on the markets and establishes the aid that may be necessary for the fisheries and aquaculture sector. i urge the commission to take all the necessary measures to help the sector, including, where appropriate, the temporary modification of the quotas allocated annually, as well as the establishment of aid, either in relation to storage - and a clear example of this need is the species of the marujito, of great importance for galicia - or in the promotion of new markets or extraordinary aid not included in the maritime and fisheries fund. the european union must act in this area immediately. both the agricultural and fisheries sectors rely on it.
madam president, i believe that the debate on this question is as necessary as the sanctions being imposed on russia for its role in the conflict in ukraine. i hope that the path of dialogue - which is clearer today than in august - will bear fruit, but the producers and processors of agricultural and fishery products cannot be the pagans of these measures. i would like to stress the fisheries sector in particular. russia imported fresh or processed fishery products from europe worth €115 million. i would like to know whether, as the commissioner announced in her blog, resources from the maritime and fisheries fund will be mobilised without further ado to compensate for these losses; whether part of the non-storageable products in the medium term can be systematically dedicated to alleviating the needs of the europeans most affected by the crisis; and finally, how the proposal on unused quotas last year will be implemented in order to improve the income expectations for the sector in 2015.

mr president, commissioner, the objectives of the neighbourhood policy are to create an area of stability, prosperity and democracy and a framework for the peaceful settlement of conflicts. this is not an easy task: the political and economic challenges facing our neighbours are enormous and our commitment to supporting a transition in these countries towards democratic societies must be stronger than ever. we have many reasons for this commitment: the pressure of migration, which is constantly increasing; the threat to our security due to the instability of the region; the energy problems which force us to look to the maghreb; or the economic potential for our economies of a mediterranean union with stable and growing countries. trade plays an essential role in this process of change: we must continue to strengthen the process of trade integration between the countries of the southern shore of the mediterranean and also between them and the european union. in negotiating these agreements, the commission must ensure an ambitious level of liberalisation in key areas such as services, investment and public procurement. at a time when much of the efforts and resources of the commission's trade and external agenda are focusing on other geographical areas, i believe that strengthening trade integrity and integration with euromed should be a priority for the european commission.
member of the commission. - mr president, the commission is aware of bolivian law no 548 on children and adolescents, adopted on 17 july 2014, which aims to ensure a high level of protection for children in bolivia. for example, unicef has commended this law for reinforcing bolivia’s commitments under ilo convention no 182 on the ‘prohibition and immediate action for the elimination of the worst forms of child labour’, which bolivia ratified in 2003. moreover, the bolivian ombudsman found that the law has strengthened the legal framework in key areas relating to the protection of children, such as infanticide, access to health and education, identity, and the right to childhood and life. however, both organisations have expressed concerns over the provisions which lowered the minimum working age for children in an apparent contradiction of bolivia’s commitments under ilo convention no 138 concerning the minimum age for admission to employment. the commission shares these concerns. we are actively engaging the bolivian government on this issue, and in parallel it is consulting the ilo to assess these provisions in the light of convention no 138. the gsp monitoring is an integral part of the revised gsp+ system and its aim is to help the commission assess gsp+ beneficiaries and the effective implementation of the gsp+ conventions. in the case of bolivia, the commission has already issued a scoreboard to bolivia in february 2014 addressing aspects of the implementation of relevant gsp+ conventions which require further work or clarification. bolivia has been cooperating with the commission and provided a reply in may 2014. following this initial exchange, the commission officially communicated with the bolivian authorities on 18 july 2014 – one day after the adoption of the bolivian law that is of concern to honourable members of the european parliament. the commission is expecting bolivia’s comments on the issue by today. the commission will review bolivia’s response and liaise with the ilo – the monitoring body for convention no 182 – before deciding on the next steps. we will keep parliament and the member states informed accordingly.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, commissioner, i agree with your prudence. i think your response has been prudent. and i think that a decision by the commission on bolivia, because of this law, would be hasty and would cause greater harm. i am in a hurry because, as you have said, we must wait for the explanation from the bolivian government, which has it. secondly, because the ilo, as you have said, is going to draw up a report which is going to be the most important report on what this violation of this fundamental convention on the right of children to work is. and thirdly, because i think that, honestly, we have to admit that the bolivian government has wanted to respond to a real problem and that is that 60% of children in bolivia work, ladies and gentlemen. and it's that, unfortunately, 90 percent of child labor in bolivia is informal, it's outside the law. the problem, of course, is that the question we all have is whether it is good to have a law protecting child labour or, on the contrary, it is better not to have one. i think we must be cautious and above all, we must respect those countries. i was appointed president of the parliament's delegation to the eurolat assembly a few days ago. i know latin america, i speak to the latin american ambassadors and they ask us not to give them lessons in democracy every day. and this is already very important. let's respect them. let's talk to them. let us work to ensure that they make progress in respecting fundamental rights. but above all - and i think it's very important to remember this - let's not condemn children in bolivia to slave labor. i think we must take this reality into account in order to make the most appropriate and prudent decision, and my group, commissioner, is with you on your words of caution and expectation.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, the regulations on child labour in bolivia are in complete breach of the relevant international conventions, both as regards employees and selfemployed workers, but it is necessary to draw attention to two points. the defence of the rights of children is a universal cause that knows no boundaries; nor should it depend on the economic power, size or interests we have in countries that allow child exploitation. on the other hand, it is very striking that a rule such as the one we are dealing with is considered in bolivia as an advance for the victims of exploitation and is also the result of an agreement with some of the organizations that associate with the minors who work, nothing less than because it makes visible and gives rights to a part of the population that, for very diverse cultural, economic or socio-political reasons, is part of the workforce of bolivia. among the children who work in that country are the more than nine hundred who are abandoned on the streets each year, adolescents who live in mistreatment or misery, and even those who consider working at ten years of age to be part of the educational process. i therefore ask whether, in addition to the sanctioning position, other actions are being considered to tackle the root of this evil in the countries where it occurs, and whether steps such as this, by making this problem visible, can contribute to solving it. i also want to know how many gsp countries have problems arising from non-compliance with the child labour convention, and how many of those aspiring to be integrated might have them.

president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, horizon 2020 is the largest framework programme for research and innovation in the european union ever established. its comhalta de chuid an choimisiúin. - a uachtaráin, tá mé buíoch gur eagraíodh díospóireacht thábhachtach den tsórt seo inniu. parliament’s decision to include a debate on the structural shortage of payments in the horizon 2020 budget is very timely, particularly just after the debate we have had already with commissioner dominik. since 2011, research and innovation programmes have suffered from a recurrent and accumulating lack of payment appropriations, and i will return to this in more detail in a few minutes. the situation has deteriorated under horizon 2020 because the payment ceilings provided for in the 2014-2020 multiannual financial framework are tight. this situation has obliged the commission to put in place drastic measures in order to meet its contractual obligations and to avoid payment delays. two key measures have been adopted already in 2013: firstly a reduction of the average pre-financing rates for all research grants; and secondly the postponement of calls for proposal closure dates, thus spreading the payment needs to later years. the implementation of these drastic measures has reduced payments by up to eur 1.5 billion in research programmes for the year 2014. we should not forget that these payment appropriation needs are, in reality, merely being pushed back to 2015 and beyond. indeed, if current trends continue, such unmet accumulated payment needs would result in more than 40% of horizon 2020 commitments remaining outstanding in 2020 and without proper payment coverage. however, these measures will no longer suffice to avoid payment delays if the requested payment appropriations are not met. in short, the approach of putting off to the future has reached its limits. concretely, for 2014 and despite the implementation of these measures, an additional eur 230 million, requested through draft amending budget 3/2014, is urgently needed before the end of the year for the research dgs to avoid payment delays. in addition to this already challenging situation, i must draw attention to the sword of damocles that hangs over horizon 2020 in the 2015 budget. the proposed 10% cut in the commission’s draft budget for research payment appropriations – representing a eur 1 billion decrease for the research budget – would lead to a situation where research dgs could fail in their contractual obligations to thousands of research beneficiaries. in practical terms, let me repeat what commissioner dominik has already mentioned to you: around 600 collaborative projects under horizon 2020 would be affected, involving more than 7000 participants, of which around 1400 are smes. i believe it is important to clarify one particular issue with regard to this proposed 10% cut in funding. some would seek to obscure the reality by presenting the situation on heading 1a as some sort of a huge increase for r&d spending by comparison with 2014. what such a narrative fails to mention is that 2014 constituted a highly atypical year in terms of the scale of the payment appropriations budget for research and innovation. indeed, in 2014, due to the phasing-in of horizon 2020, some 15% less has been budgeted by comparison with 2013. the ‘increased spending’ narrative neglects two important factors: the step increase of the commitment profile in the last years of the seventh framework programme (fp7), as fp7 was backloaded; and, secondly, the overall limited availability of payments which we face. thus, 2014 cannot be used as a valid benchmark for judging the budget trend in 2015. in fact, 60% of our spending in 2014 and 2015 is actually legacy-related payments from fp7, meaning that the full roll-out of horizon 2020 is, de facto, being pushed even further into the future due to the lack of payment appropriations. in short, an outcome which provided for a cut in spending on the scale originally proposed by the commission for 2015 would seriously call into question the reputation of the european union as a reliable funder of research. this is a dramatic situation for a flagship policy that is intended to support jobs, growth and competitiveness. it is also highly regrettable in the current economic situation, given our collective search for growth-enhancing measures and knowing that research and innovation are crucial to new growth and jobs. such artificially low investment in research will also negatively impact on other initiatives such as the digital agenda, the energy technologies plan and our climate change policies. such a large cut in 2015 would, moreover, be at odds with repeated affirmations in support of the europe 2020 growth and jobs agenda, most recently articulated through the strategic agenda for the union in times of change. it goes without saying, therefore, that a new boost for jobs, growth and investment cannot be achieved if we continue to reduce planned investments in research and innovation. we are counting on you, the members of the european parliament, to give us your active support in addressing this problem by adopting without modification both draft amending budget 3/2014 and the draft budget for 2015 as presented by the commission.
