mr guerrero, we are being so cautious in this presidency that we have not accepted more than two blue cards in this debate at one time. you will, therefore, understand that we are trying by all means to save time so that your time is yours and no one else's.
mr president, shortly before the summer the european union experienced one of those 'outbreaks of complacency' that we have been witnessing for some years now: the end of the crisis was virtually decreed. but after the summer, it turns out that it seems possible that we're entering a third depression: the oecd has revised growth, and growth is worse for the euro area and for the three big economies in the euro area. why is this happening? because we have turned the european economy into a chronic sickness. a chronic patient to whom we have only given immunosuppressants - austerity at all costs, social cuts, the brake on investment and wage devaluation - and what the european union needs at the moment - the euro economy - is a vitamin shock, a vitamin shock with investment, with growth, with education and with the recovery of the wage level, the loss of which, as has been pointed out, not by the 'friends of the deficit', but by the international monetary fund, the oecd, the world bank and various think tanks, is at the origin of the devaluation of demand as well. without demand there will be no economic recovery; without investment there will be no growth in the european union. without investment and without demand, poverty will continue and a mass of workers will continue to be created who, despite receiving a salary, live below the poverty line.
mr president, i think it is fair to welcome the measures announced by mr draghi, president of the ecb, but let us not be fooled: the european central bank is not going to solve the enormous problems we have. the european central bank will give us time to solve the problems so that we can make the necessary reforms and start creating jobs and economic growth. spain is one example. an example of a reformist country. and it's an example because it's the country that has the most growth in the euro area and it's the country that is creating the most jobs. it is not enough, we are convinced of it. but we have no doubt that it is an example. commissioner, we need not only reforms, but also we need to implement the juncker plan. i hope that this time those plans which we have so often announced will not fall through the cracks and that we will soon see them implemented.
mr president, the measures we are taking at each summit support two ideas: that only from a common position can we face global challenges and that we cannot continue to substitute patches for the construction of economic and political governance. we must either opt for a euro area with a growth model based on the real economy and social development, or we will no longer be the benchmark of progress that we have been for decades. we therefore need binding medium- and long-term measures that are the backbone of europe, investments with european added value in infrastructure and transport that add competitiveness, and shared minimum standards in social policy. these policies must be implemented in a coordinated way in all the member states because everything else is fireworks and political dishonesty. not doing so, commissioner, answers the question you asked about why private investment is being stopped. either we do this, or we will not get out of this economic crisis.
mr president, mr katainen, ladies and gentlemen of the council, after the disastrous economic data this summer, with the three main economies of the euro area in technical unemployment, you have come here today to convey to us once again your blind faith in the combination of austerity and structural reforms. they basically propose that we accelerate, mr katainen, faster and faster towards the precipice. today he insisted again that the problem is that the reforms are not moving fast enough. and now, after the reforms you have imposed on the peripheral countries - spain, greece and portugal - you are going to do the same, or you intend to do the same with france and italy: further reduction of wages, more flexibility in the labour market and further reduction of public service expenditure. meanwhile, the casino economy continues to ride on a european central bank whose liquidity is trapped in the hands of speculators, as my colleague said earlier. mr. katainen, how long is this going to go on? please admit that you were wrong, apologize for the suffering caused and, once and for all, relaunch that investment plan you promised and of which today, frankly, you have told us absolutely nothing. and because we don't have it, we don't even have a date for the euro summit yet. so please, make a 180-degree turn, admit the mistake and change this economic policy that is leading us to suicide.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i would have liked to have had a comprehensive debate with members but my flight to the australia g20 meeting is leaving in a few minutes’ time so i have to rush. i would just like to make a couple of comments. mr balz recalled reforms in order to strengthen growth potential. this is a very important issue, because in many of our member states the potential for growth is at a low level. this is why we need various reforms. it depends on the country. we do not need the same reforms in every country, but it depends on the local situation. it is very easy to agree with ms rodrigues, who said that we have to emphasise safeguarding the european social model. she also recalled the need for reforms to strengthen innovation, for instance. this is very important. there are various ways to organise innovation financing in different member states, and we could perhaps copy the best practices from different countries. this is something which could renew europe, and this kind of reform brings us forward. there are many strengths in europe but also some shortages and weaknesses. i personally believe in research and development and innovation. innovation usually means that there must be strong fundamental research and entrepreneurship. so it is not only a question of money but also of how to organise and use public resources better than we are doing at the moment. it is also very important to find a more efficient way to use the eib. mr lucke – if i understood correctly – said that, if we want investment, it does not make sense to consolidate. for me this is not a black and white question, because investment means demand and that there must be a good level of confidence. that is why we have to combine healthy reforms. we need more demand and some consolidation in order to strengthen confidence, and we need european efforts. the commissioners-designate are trying to define this at the moment. i hope that we can continue this debate later on, focusing more on investment and growth.
president of the council. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for the opportunity you have given me and the presidency to hear the wide range of views on this subject. the talks went far beyond the specific theme of the euro summit meeting next month. i cannot add much to what i said in my opening speech about that particular meeting. i can assure you that we will be able to say more when the meeting is called. we can certainly have a more detailed discussion at the plenary next month. i would just like to reiterate, in relation to the broad issues of growth and investment that have been raised, that the italian presidency regards as a priority and with extreme urgency the subject and the issues that have been discussed with different positions expressed by the groups and individual members and, in conclusion, i would like to say that i have taken good note of all the points and all the indications that have emerged in this discussion and i will ensure that these points and these indications are conveyed to all the people involved in the preparation of the next euro summit.
in writing. it is disappointing to see how the commission continues to be blind to the reality, not of the data but of the millions of people in europe who, after experiencing firsthand the failure of austerity and structural reforms, continue to face a scenario of lack of economic growth, long-term unemployment, job insecurity, wage devaluation and social deprivation that leads to poverty and exclusion. we need facts. we demand a specific timetable for the investment plan proposed by president juncker, but also commitments from the european leaders on the financial resources they intend to commit to this plan at national but above all at european level. we need expansionary and supportive fiscal policies to stimulate a sclerotic demand which, together with the deflation that is stalking us, condemns us to permanent stagnation. and we need to stop cutting wages, because even the oecd warns us that this has become a problem that can condemn us for many years. we need to dispel the myth of expansionary austerity because expansion is impossible when everyone is saving at once and no one is spending or investing, and it only causes poverty and suffering.
madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen of the italian presidency, i have been here for two months and i already have the feeling that i am listening to a little scratched disc. some things: on the implementation of the youth guarantee; we have already discussed on a number of occasions that some countries are applying the youth guarantee badly, in contradiction to the commission's own recommendations. in spain it is only being used as a receptacle for funds to be distributed between companies. there are no training programmes, no support and counselling systems, no supplementary support systems for young people who have no income whatsoever. is the commission planning to do anything about this? and, by the way, in spain, too, very constructive measures are being taken, such as the abolition of the youth council, which the government has done in recent days. the second element is the question of resources. will there be more resources? we know that six billion euros is not enough. thirdly, and this is a comment to the italian presidency: frankly, it seems a bad joke that they come here to tell us that they have not been able to find a date for the summit. it is not that we are genuine fans of summits - because we know that they are often held to talk and not decide anything, which is what young people have had to witness in recent years - but that they have not been able, in the programme of the presidency, to find a date for a summit on an issue which is, fundamentally, one of the most serious problems there is at the moment here in the european union, such as youth unemployment, which seems, frankly, very unimportant.
madam president, mr andor, thank you very much for your work during this time in the commission. i thank you for the courage to take forward an innovative and ambitious initiative such as the youth guarantee, which we must not forget is based on a successful experience, that of austria and finland, and therefore it is even more important that there is a guarantee of success in the countries that are going to join it and that are implementing it. but this is a matter of particular concern to me and that is why i ask the commission and the council to insist on monitoring the implementation of the funds in countries such as spain, which is, as you know, sadly the leader in youth unemployment with almost 54%, because spain receives half the funds of this programme. it is particularly important that we ensure that the use of funds, especially for training, is not subject to fraudulent use as we have seen in madrid and andalusia. it is important that we ask that countries which have to be exemplary in the implementation of a programme like this, such as spain, are not only well supervised, but are required to be a reference.
madam president, we have 5.2 million young people out of work, a figure that is fast-talking but which is extremely painful for this continent: 23%. more than half of young people in some countries, such as spain, croatia or greece. and this is not just data, it has enormous economic consequences, because we're wasting talent and enormous investments in public education; enormous social consequences, because we're condemning an entire generation to poverty, emigration or precariousness; and also enormous institutional consequences, because we're disconnecting them from their institutions. we have given some answers - it is always good to give answers - but these answers - the youth guarantee, an initiative for youth employment - have been slow, unambitious, timid, and are being misused by some states - very important: the case of spain is flagrant with the youth guarantee - and, moreover, we are conditioning the states and the budgets of the states by accounting for these budgets. what we have to do is to give an ambitious response, commensurate with the scar that this problem is causing for the future of this continent. ambitious, fast and urgent, because the future is calling us to the door.
madam president, the initiative to promote youth employment which we approved a few months ago was a very important step towards tackling one of the great and fundamental challenges facing europe, and we must take care, precisely for this reason, to ensure that the expectations and objectives we set ourselves are met, namely that young people can be better trained and have a decent job. the rate of youth unemployment is a problem of concern to all, but mainly to certain countries and regions. let me refer today specifically to the outermost regions of the european union, which always have the most difficulty in all areas and also in finding job opportunities for their young people. we are talking about unemployment in europe at 10%, in the canary islands at 33.7% and in réunion at 29%. in the case of youth unemployment, in the canary islands we had, at the end of 2013, a rate of 62%, a frightening figure. we're getting better, yes, but there's still a lot to do.
madam president, one of the greatest challenges facing the european union is precisely to open the doors of the labour market to young people. in the case of spain, 40% of the unemployed are under the age of 30, i.e. 1.5 million. if it is one of the biggest problems facing the european union, we have to be ambitious in the response. youth guarantee is an answer, but it is not ambitious. it's not satisfying, it's not effective, it's not enough. we must therefore consider what policies should be implemented to respond and not frustrate generations who have a very dark present, but who also have no hopes or expectations for the future. we need to be more ambitious. we must break with this austerity policy. we must increase investment policy, growth policy. we must talk about the industrialization of europe. we must talk about jobs, to give a new horizon and prospects to a generation that may be lost.
madam president, the problem of youth unemployment requires, in addition to solving the economic imbalances we have been talking about this morning, more funding, closer links between training and demand for new skills and professions, better conditions for the first jobs and the promotion of self-employment. we have a deficit in some of the technical-scientific specialties on which innovation depends that urgently needs to be addressed. but i also miss a speech on values and attitudes. it's not comfortable to talk about this, but there is a responsibility on the part of authorities, individuals and families. we must promote other role models, educate in responsibility, teach failure and restore the prestige of personal effort. knowledge yields more with values. soulless talent, as we've seen with unscrupulous financiers, is what's driving this crisis, and this is the best example of what i'm saying and why we need to change.
madam president, the deterioration of the labour market cannot be solved by initiatives like this, which argue that the problem is the lack of employability of our young people. i have been a vocational training teacher and a job counsellor, ladies and gentlemen, and i will tell you what the problem is with our young people: when we have to help our young people to find employment, the problem is not that they are not sufficiently trained or that they are not sufficiently flexible. the problem is there are no jobs. and we know this well in the southern european countries, because our labour market has been torn apart to obey the dictates of the big financial institutions and the big multinationals. and when they say that the alternative is self-employment, it is laughable, because most of our young people are living in dramatic situations and do not have the start-up capital to meet the costs of starting a new business, when, moreover, most small businesses are suffering the consequences of the economic situation. the reality is that young people today are faced with unemployment, precariousness or exile, and that the deterioration of the labour market is solved by developing a model... in writing. - i voted in favour of this report which introduces amendments to the legal framework for the european globalisation adjustment funds. in particular, the minimum number of unemployed persons eligible for the fund has been reduced from 500 to 200, the financing of the state's share of the fund has been made easier for those states which have social, economic or financial constraints, the regions' leading role in implementing the fund has been increased and the eagf's budget has been increased, since it will be integrated into the eu's ordinary budget. i have therefore voted in favour.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report which introduces amendments to the legal framework for the european globalisation adjustment funds. in particular, the minimum number of unemployed persons eligible for the fund has been reduced from 500 to 200, the financing of the state's share of the fund has been made easier for those states which have social, economic or financial constraints, the regions' leading role in implementing the fund has been increased and the eagf's budget has been increased, since it will be integrated into the eu's ordinary budget. i have therefore voted in favour.
in writing. - the egf is a tool for the relocation of workers made redundant in sectors particularly affected by 'globalisation'. to this end, it allocates most of the funds to training, mentoring, support and development of "personal skills", while only a tiny portion of it goes directly into the pockets of the workers and only if they obediently follow the proposed itinerary or in the unlikely event that they get a job as a result of the programme. the positive vote is explained by the recognition that any help directed to those individuals and families who are suffering is welcome. it does not in any way imply acceptance of the paternalistic and unjust logic underlying the design of this fund. people who have lost their jobs have not lost their jobs because of lack of training and certainly do not need "incentives" to learn computer science or to look for work. they have lost it because the economy and the productive fabric have been severely undermined by powers that never consulted them and that only seek the private benefit of a tiny minority.

in writing. - we announce our vote in favour of the motion for a resolution on the mobilisation of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) in connection with the proposed implementation of technical assistance needs at the initiative of the commission. i would like to express my full agreement with the commission on the need to improve the means of better informing potential beneficiaries and to extend the mobilisation of these funds, and we particularly agree with the new measures proposed, such as special attention to unemployed young people under 25 who are not currently in any education or training programme (neet). we also think it is right to increase assistance at regional and local level, extending the scope of the egf, since it allows access to it from regions and municipalities with a lower population density. finally, we want to support the motion for a resolution on the requirement for more financial resources and less conditionality for access to the market.

in writing. - we announce our vote in favour of the motion for a resolution on the mobilisation of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) in connection with the proposed implementation for the accommodation, food and drink services sector in aragon. this sector has suffered a sharp decline in recent years, even exceeding the decline suffered by the sector in the whole of spain. the sharp reduction in production has had negative consequences in the form of redundancies and closures of enterprises which have dragged other sectors of activity in aragon. in view of the situation, it is absolutely necessary and appropriate to use the fund to help redundant workers to be re-trained in other sectors of activity, to supplement their subsistence and to encourage self-employment.
in writing. - the european union has established this instrument to provide additional support to workers suffering from the consequences of major structural changes in global business models or who are made redundant as a result of the global economic and financial crisis, and to assist them with their reintegration into the labour market. the spanish government, aware of the difficult situation in certain sectors, requested a financial contribution from the egf following the redundancies of 904 workers in 661 enterprises operating in nace revision 2 division 56 (food and drink) in the autonomous community of aragon. the programme is worth €960,000 for training and retraining, job search assistance, guidance on reintegration into work and career support for dependent persons. i have therefore voted in favour of this important aid.

in writing. - we announce our vote in favour of the motion for a resolution on the mobilisation of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) in connection with the proposed application for the carpentry and furniture sector in castile and león. the sector has lost 40% of its exports since 2008, almost three times the average european drop. this slump in sales has had a negative impact on production, leading to layoffs and factory closures in a region which, due to its low population density and low industrial sector, is particularly affected by the problem of industrial unemployment. the measures of reintegration into employment, vocational guidance and intensive job search support are not only welcome but also essential to alleviate the crisis experienced in the region in recent years.
in writing. - on 22 july 2014, the commission adopted a proposal for a decision on the mobilisation of the european globalisation adjustment fund for spain to support the reintegration into the labour market of workers made redundant in three enterprises operating in nace division 16 (wood and cork industry, except furniture; manufacture of basketware and spartanware) in the region of castile and león, following major structural changes in world trade patterns as a result of globalisation. the programme is to provide eur 700 000 for reception and information sessions, career guidance and counselling, support for intensive job search, training, entrepreneurship promotion and incentives. i would like to thank my colleague, mr esteban gonzález pons, for this report, which i voted in favour of.

i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, we do not know how many people have already died from ebola. the health systems in west africa are very weak and are now totally collapsed, with a ratio of two doctors per 100,000 inhabitants to deal with an unprecedented epidemic, as the commissioner has rightly said. and the european union and its member states have no choice but to cut the budget for development aid. my country, spain, for example, has cut it by 74% since 2011. development aid is not charity, gentlemen, it is justice. and the european countries have a huge debt to the african countries. and i'm not going to talk about the resource plundering that we continue to commit on that continent. but it seems that the people of the south are not the priority even in situations of extreme need. we need to get it to become a global threat so we can get going. but this europe, which is dedicated to the defence of human rights, does not give priority to the real needs of this situation. there are no doctors, technicians, laboratories, isolation units, training for the population and overwhelmed health bodies. they don't need military support. let us follow the example of cuba, which will send 165 highly specialized doctors, and not that of the united states, which proposes to send 3,000 soldiers under the pretext of supporting the development of a health structure. more soldiers than medics. enough conflict is already being suffered by these people to further militarize the region. a european plan is urgently needed to mobilise the resources needed to provide effective health care now. we can't wait any longer.
mr president, the african continent is typically and topically called the 'continent of pain' but in this case the topic corresponds to reality. the combination of famine and genocide has taken the lives of millions of people on that continent. poverty, lack of access to water, lack of education and infant mortality affect hundreds of thousands of people. on that continent, on the other hand, there is armed violence, there is terrorism, there are civil conflicts everywhere. a continent that a few decades ago abandoned the situation of colonialism, but which is now being colonized in its resources and in its structures. the ebola crisis has now been unleashed on that continent. the ebola crisis, as commissioner georgieva has pointed out, has three characteristics: an exponential growth in the number of people affected; a very high death rate, around 60%, and, on the other hand, also the lack of health structures with which these countries can deal with the problem. and that's our challenge: to provide, of course, structures; to provide medical supplies; and to allow humanitarian access. i therefore believe that it is time to support the milan council, to support the united nations meeting and finally to support the decision of the donors on this matter on 24 september. a final word: the sooner the european countries ratify the 11th european development fund, the more funds we will have to respond structurally to this problem.
mr president, sierra leone, liberia, guinea conakry and other countries are suffering from an ebola epidemic. but it's not just this that's destroying thousands of lives. ebola is accompanied by poverty. they are suffering the consequences of being poor countries, of being impoverished countries. the european union, the united states, the west, have turned their backs on the ebola outbreaks in africa for years and only when they saw that the virus could reach europe and that our high walls and our fences at the borders could not stop it, only then did they react. not to save the citizens of these african countries, but to save themselves. and it seems that all lives are not worth the same. big pharmaceutical companies don't care about the diseases of the poor. they don't give benefits. and this voracity of the economic elites is as lethal as ebola. and i think it is important to highlight - and the european parliament should welcome this - the announcement by cuba to send personnel. this is the largest announcement of aid in the form of personnel to fight ebola: one hundred and sixty-five people, including medical and nursing staff. cuba, once again, demonstrates its international solidarity.
mr president, my first words can only be of support for the victims of ebola, and i want to extend this support to all the people who are working on the ground, risking their lives to save those who live in countries without the minimum health structures to guarantee the response this epidemic needs. one of them was spanish priest miguel pajares, who died after contracting the disease in liberia while helping the most needy, in this case ebola patients, who are currently repudiated by their community even after being cured. according to the world health organization, ebola is a public health emergency that requires a coordinated international response. in this race we must be faster than this silent enemy who has already claimed 2300 lives. the situation, ladies and gentlemen, is deteriorating rapidly and ebola is affecting the weak economies of the region and, consequently, public order. humanitarian needs are increasing and if they are not met, it will be much more difficult to combat this disease. the number of patients is growing much faster than our ability to manage it. we know that the commission has increased humanitarian aid, but it must also increase the help of experts in the region. all countries must be involved in research, not forgetting the measures to prevent the spread of this epidemic, without condemning these countries, already severely punished, to lose all hope of getting out of poverty as a result of their isolation. and i end by reminding those who care for these ebola patients, that they deserve all of our recognition whether they are american, whether they are european, whether they are african. they are our heroes, anonymous heroes, and to them we owe not only our attention, as we are giving it here today, but also our action, and fast.

efforts by providing an additional €10 million to counter the crisis. this has brought the eu's overall humanitarian budget for iraq to €17 million since the beginning of the year. in addition, member states have contributed a further eur 40 million for humanitarian aid. the eu civil protection mechanism has also been activated to facilitate humanitarian assistance. the european union has provided mr president, the work that the european union is doing to advance its values and principles at international level is undeniable. the union's external relations policy has as one of its main objectives the universality of human rights throughout the world: the world looks to us to defend them and we cannot let them down. but there are many countries where fundamental rights are violated and where many people are not guaranteed them. the lack of freedom to practice one's religion is a clear example of these human rights violations. we are faced daily with the continuing massacres of minorities in iraq and syria, with a particular effect on the christian community, whose members are forced to renounce their religion or else they are exterminated. christians in the east look to us with the desperation of those who need to be protected. the archbishop of baghdad told us during his last visit to this parliament: 'we need help not because we are christians, but because we are human beings'. i welcome the fact that this report deals with the negative impact of the increasing terrorist acts in iraq, but i do not see a greater commitment to the consequences of terrorism in the world, including europe. this report is full of abuses in the fight against terrorism, and it is necessary to point out where they exist, but i must say that the text should express a stronger condemnation of the global rise of terrorism and make clearer references to the victims of terrorism. it is therefore unbalanced in my view. human rights mean nothing to terrorists: they feed on barbarism and utter disregard for human life. examples of this are the cases of the boko haram girls in nigeria; the kidnapping of religious minority girls in iraq, who are used as sex slaves; or the atrocious murders of journalists and aid workers who were doing humanitarian work. i ask the international community not to let down its guard in the face of the escalation of terrorism we are experiencing, because only together can we say loud and clear to the terrorists that we love freedom and life more than they love repression and death.
madam president, i have heard a report full of good intentions. it's something i celebrate. the fact is that i could give many examples of european union interests being put above human rights. in this case, i'm going to talk about something that affects us in my country. that is the situation with morocco. as i have seen, morocco is the country which benefits most from its relationship with the european union. it also has an advanced status. and although the european union's agreements are conditional on respect for human rights, morocco is committing serious violations of international law and human rights. for example, in the sahara, where it is an occupying power and where it is in breach of the united nations mandate, delaying and hindering the process of decolonisation. it is also committing very serious attacks against the population of the occupied territories. it's funny, before tunisia there was an arab spring in the sahara and we didn't know anything. for example, the prisoners of gdeim izik's group of the dignity camps, sentenced in february 2013 by a moroccan military court: 25 civilians tried; eight sentenced to life imprisonment; four to thirty years and four to twenty-five years. it's funny, when do we care about civil movements? only when they're enemy countries. it is not about changing the moroccan regime, but about cooperation to improve governance. they are not required to respect human rights, but are given recommendations. i hope we will take this into account in the trade agreements.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen of the commission, i believe in your work; i believe that what you are doing is important. we're not perfect; there are a lot of contradictions, but that's the way the world evolves. i believe that you are doing an important job in ensuring that europe remains a beacon of civilization in the world. and i want to give you two pieces of advice on latin america which i think are particularly important. first, i think it is very important that european companies that invest and work in this world that has globalized production, that invest and work in latin america, do so respecting the labor rights and environmental rights of the communities where they operate. we have serious problems in latin america because of the way many european companies are acting. i would recommend that we look at the problems in this area because, as mr howitt said, corporate social responsibility is very important in the culture of respect for human rights throughout the world. and secondly, i think that our eyes, our ears are aware of the human rights violations by the ngos, by the thousands of volunteers, by the thousands of people who work all over the world, also in latin america - europeans and latin americans - in defence of human rights. they have to get our help; they have to get our support. i think this is a second important piece of advice for making a second report, next year, even better.
madam president, the truth is that i can think of few sets of principles more important than human rights and i think it is very important that reports be made on them. i am surprised at the way the european union is looking at this issue, always looking outwards and so little inwards. it is very good that we monitor the observance of human rights beyond our borders, but perhaps it would also be interesting to look a little inward. look a little bit at the people with disabilities, the people who lose their homes, the people who can't put the heating in in the winter, the people who are looking for food in the containers, the immigrants who are locked up in detention centers... we could also possibly use a report on these human rights violations.
madam president, i give you my best wishes. some 12 years ago i had the opportunity to work in this house as an assistant, particularly on the peace process in the great lakes countries, including burundi, following the serious conflicts of the 1990s. at the beginning of this century, it seemed that the longed-for peace and reconciliation brought about by the arusha accords was taking hold. but the situation is getting worse, as is shown by the fact that we are dealing with today: the arrest of pierre claver mbonimpa and others for denouncing, as did the local office of the united nations, the youth training centres of the ruling party. 2015 is an election year in burundi and these events cause us added concern, by the intimidating situation towards opposition parties and by the use of the judiciary to exclude political competitors. it is appropriate to make an electoral observation: the cotonou agreement and the international covenant on civil and political rights bind and oblige the burundian government. the institutions of the european union, and this parliament in particular, must always raise our voices in defence of those who are deprived of their voice and call today, in this case, on the burundian government for the immediate release of mr mbonimpa and for full respect for human rights and freedom of expression.
i would remind you that we are here in this hall, which represents the most democratic institution of the european union, and i do not think it is appropriate for you to make such statements. please apologize. (closure of the 'catch the eye' procedure)
member of the commission. - madam president, i welcome the opportunity provided by this emergency resolution to address the case of pierre claver mbonimpa. we attach great importance to his situation, which has received considerable attention in our dialogue with the burundian authorities. as you know, protecting and encouraging human rights defenders is one of the major priorities of the overall eu policy on human rights and democracy. human rights defenders have a vital moral and practical role to play in giving confidence to civil society organisations and to citizens wishing to assert their rights and enjoy their fundamental freedoms in challenging circumstances. the arrest of mr mbonimpa gave us cause for significant concern. the eu expressed that concern strongly, underlining to the burundian authorities that the legal and human rights of the accused should be scrupulously and transparently respected. we also reacted publicly to the misguided decision to keep mr mbonimpa in pre-trial detention. the eu delegation and the eu member states represented in bujumbura have been in close contact with mr mbonimpa’s lawyer. just a few days ago we were informed that he had been sent to hospital. naturally we will continue to enquire about the conditions under which he is being treated and about his state of health. we must also continue to insist that his rights are fully respected. the world is watching this case as a test of the respect in practice for rights and freedoms in burundi. in burundi, and throughout the world, the eu has spoken out against any measures that encourage the perception of politically motivated justice. experience shows that this perception in itself is dangerous and destabilising. it is regrettable that mr mbonimpa’s case should need to be assessed in such a context and even more so that it comes against a background of other apparent breaches of judicial standards and of increasing tension ahead of the elections in 2015. these threats command continued attention and response. the cotonou agreement is about dialogue of equals and we will not hesitate to raise our concerns. the eu is fully committed to accompanying and supporting burundi in its peace-building process and democratisation. promotion and respect for human rights and the development of an independent and reliable justice system are, of course, at the core of this action. through the european instrument for democracy and human rights and the european development fund we are supporting actions against discrimination and violence in the country and promoting a diverse and constructive burundian civil society, including for the lgbti communities. the local, legislative and presidential elections in 2015 are an important test for the stability of burundi as well as its democratisation. it is important that the un also follows the situation closely in cooperation with the eu. effective monitoring of human rights by the international community must continue during and after the elections. the eu, in close coordination with the member states represented in bujumbura, will continue to follow this case and take the necessary steps as the situation evolves.

the next item on the agenda is the debate on six motions for resolutions on human rights violations in bangladesh [2014/2834 ((rsp) ].
the commission has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the report by mr bangemann. however, the situation remains worrying. 2013 and 2014 have been tumultuous and unstable, with elections boycotted by the main opposition party, demonstrations violently suppressed, arbitrary arrests and enforced disappearances. to this must be added the deplorable situation of human rights defenders and journalists who are engaged in self-censorship in a country that ranks 146th out of 180 in the reporters without borders press freedom ranking. the number of people on death row is also worrying, some 10 000 of them. the european union should insist on promoting the defence of human rights as a value in itself, but also that political instability in bangladesh could have dire consequences on the economic growth the country has been experiencing over the last ten years, frustrating its chances of meeting the millennium development goals and its aspiration to move from a low-income country to a middle-income one by 2021, the 50th anniversary of its independence. poverty and democratic deficits undermine the rights of bangladesh's citizens and can be a breeding ground for extremist movements, which is especially worrying in the world's second largest muslim country, 90 per cent of its 150 million people. this danger is heightened by the call made in early september by al qaeda leader ayman al zawahiri for the establishment of an islamic caliphate in bangladesh, myanmar and parts of india. we must send a clear message. we welcome bangladesh's progress towards the millennium development goals and acknowledge its steps in the right direction, for example by preventing child marriages, but we must continue to insist that strong action is taken to ensure freedom of expression and political freedoms.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's citizens are not subject to the death penalty. in bangladesh, 87% of work is informal and therefore without social or labour rights. in the textile sector, wages are far below those in the countries around it and agreements are systematically breached by the exporting multinationals, who reap the maximum benefits from this situation. we must demand that the commitments to respect the rights of workers, and especially of women workers, who are subject to conditions of exploitation at work, be respected. the ban on trade unions in export processing areas, where working conditions, health and safety are extremely poor, must be lifted. the compulsory mechanism for compensating the 1 100 dead and 2 500 injured in rana plaza who have not yet been compensated must be put into operation. it is the need and duty of this parliament and the member states to denounce publicly the multinationals which have failed to comply with the victims and to exclude from aid and public procurement those companies which violate human and labour rights.

in writing. - the ebola virus has spread to guinea and four other countries (liberia, nigeria, sierra leone and senegal) and has affected almost 4 000 people, causing more than 2 000 deaths, and whereas there are also unconfirmed cases of ebola infection and fatalities. the who acknowledges that the outbreak has been underestimated and estimates that the number of patients could exceed 20,000 over the next three months. the commission should therefore carry out a needs assessment and draw up country-specific plans. it is also very important that information and education actions are undertaken to raise awareness of the symptoms and preventive measures, in order to facilitate the confidence and cooperation of people with the anti-ebola measures, as information and communication are an important aspect of the fight against this disease. finally, the member states and the commission must also coordinate and strengthen medical research and the production of effective drugs and vaccines against the ebola virus and promote the necessary clinical trials.
in writing. - the positive vote in favour of the resolution proposed by the european parliament on the european response to the ebola outbreak which is striking tragically is the least we can do in response to the tragedy which is taking place in west africa. we cannot stand by while people suffer. the humanism which underpins the construction of europe must stimulate us to give a firm and comprehensive response to human suffering. the union is a peace project which has brought our continent the greatest social progress in centuries, and which has brought us to the present state of well-being, and it is our moral obligation, by reason of history, by reason of our values, to help people who suffer. we must therefore also urge the member states to increase aid, not only in money but also in equipment, to the countries affected by this human tragedy. the european union should also be able to provide a more rapid and more effective response in the field of humanitarian aid by strengthening the links of integration.
in writing. - in its paragraph 3, the resolution suggests that 'the possibility of using military and civil defence assets' be examined in order to respond to the crisis. the resolution, in paragraph 4, also supports and encourages the recent increase in commitments by the commission in support of the african union's aseowa mission, which is not only a civilian but also a military mission. that is why i voted against this resolution. the ebola epidemic, since it was officially declared on 22 march in guinea, has spread to four other countries (liberia, nigeria, sierra leone and senegal), affecting nearly 4000 people and causing over 2000 deaths. international efforts to date have been dramatically inadequate. the interest of the majority of meps in this matter is welcome: a european plan is urgently needed to mobilise the resources needed by the member states for the delivery of effective humanitarian aid, in particular to provide specialist medical staff and technical equipment, such as mobile laboratories, which promote early warning and isolation cells to slow down the rate of contagion. if such a plan includes military elements it will be ineffective and rejected.

mr president, a case of contagion in europe that is healing does not show the power of ebola, not the full power of ebola. the power of ebola is reflected in thousands and thousands of citizens in africa who cannot be cured. ebola is cured with hygiene and medicine, not politics. spain reacted with professionalism and seriousness to a contagion, which occurred in madrid, of a volunteer, a heroine: teresa romero. and today, thanks to the spanish health services, he is in the process of healing. we're not always going to get it. so it's very important that we be clear that, in the face of this disease, our lack of solidarity could trigger a global pandemic: our lack of solidarity alone. we must give europe peace of mind, but we must give africa hope. barriers and controls alone will not save europe from ebola. if we do not save africa, it is impossible to save europe: we must go where the problem is, and we must tell the citizens the truth.

president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to have the opportunity to take part this morning in the debate on the european semester. i have examined the draft resolution which forms the basis of this debate and i am impressed by the wide range of issues it deals with and the importance of the issues it addresses. in fact, the debate this morning goes beyond the mechanics of economic coordination. we are here to discuss how europe conducts its economic policy, its employment policy and all the other policies which contribute to employment and growth. the resolution focuses on the implementation of the priorities for 2014: implementation is key; we already have strategic guidelines at the level of the european union, the conclusions of the european council and, for each member state, country-specific recommendations. the implementation of these recommendations requires bold structural reforms, including in areas of national competence, which sometimes conflict with acquired rights. the benefits are slow to appear, which in turn increases political pressure. the council is strongly encouraging the member states to undertake such reforms. this debate is about the priorities for 2014, but we must recognise that the european semester is not and cannot be an exercise in which priorities change radically from one year to the next. some details may change from one year to the next, but the priorities themselves fall within a longer time horizon. that is what the presidency is doing this autumn. let us look at the european semester in the wider context of the europe 2020 strategy and its mid-term review. the review should also strengthen the link between all the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy and the european semester. that is why the presidency has launched a political reflection at council level on the mid-term review of the europe 2020 strategy. we decided from the outset that all the parties concerned should be involved in this exercise, including, for example, those involved in areas such as agriculture, culture and cohesion. the exercise is still ongoing, but i would like to take this opportunity to highlight some of the initial results. first, all the debates so far have confirmed the importance of keeping the europe 2020 strategy's focus on jobs and growth. the second message is about ambition. despite the significant progress made, particularly in energy and education, we must recognize that we are not on track in all areas. employment in particular is a matter of grave concern. but the fact that progress is not enough does not mean that we should pursue less ambitious goals. the third message is about strengthening governance. policy directions issued in the context of the european semester can sometimes be bitter pills. but i'm glad to say that no one wants to weaken the semester. in fact, we should rather try to streamline the process and improve the outcomes. we must also ensure that all those who have to implement reforms are included in the process. this includes not only governments but also parliaments and other stakeholders, both at national and european union level. let me say a few words about the sectoral contributions to this debate. on competitiveness, the council confirmed in september that the single market and industrial competitiveness must be firmly integrated into the europe 2020 strategy. in particular, in the field of research and innovation, which play a key role in europe's economic recovery, the quality of investment in research and innovation is as essential as the level of spending. we must do more to promote a european research area. in the field of economic policy, the council's approach is based on three pillars which represent a combination of measures to be implemented simultaneously and jointly by the member states. the first is structural reform, which i have already mentioned and which is closely linked to the second. the second is investment, which is a key priority for the italian presidency, and the third is the need to build confidence through a differentiated budgetary policy geared to growth and respect for the stability and growth pact, while making use of the flexibility inherent in its rules. the council welcomes president-elect juncker's announcement that he will present an investment initiative within the first three months of his mandate. investment will help to boost demand in the short term, but will also help to increase the growth potential of the economy in the long term. as regards employment and social affairs, the council discussed the europe 2020 strategy last week, and the italian presidency brought together heads of state at the beginning of october to find solutions to the problem of unemployment, but this concerns the in-depth debate we had in the previous point. in this regard, i would draw your attention to the letter signed by 22 member states, with the support of the italian presidency, which stresses the need for better integration of gender equality in the revised strategy. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have outlined the main points of our work so far. the ministers for the environment, cohesion, education, culture, transport, energy and telecommunications will also be making their contribution. we shall then summarize the situation and prepare a report for the general affairs council in december. we hope that this joint political reflection will be useful to the new commission when it prepares its proposals for the mid-term review. thank you for your attention.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, let me start by thanking the rapporteur, mr philippe de backer, and all the other members for their valuable contribution to parliament’s report on the european semester. this report is a timely and important contribution to the topical debate on economic governance in the eu. the report touches upon a wide range of issues, many of which are related to parliament’s expectations of the commission in the future. provided that parliament confirms the new college tomorrow, the new commission can be in place at the beginning of november. so we are currently in the middle of transition. i therefore hope you understand that here today i will not be in a position to answer all your questions related to the future actions of the new commission. however, i can assure you that this does not mean that we are not listening. on the contrary, we have taken into consideration the points you have raised in the report. i can also assure you that this will have the attention of the new commission. i fully agree with you that the most pressing challenge ahead of us is to create sustainable growth and generate jobs. the european semester has been an extremely useful exercise in identifying and coordinating policy responses to the challenges faced by individual member states and the eu as a whole. the member states are adjusting to the reinforced coordination process and common rules we built together in the depths of the crisis. the semester has proven to be fundamental in presenting incentives for significant fiscal and structural reforms in the member states. these are the very reforms that are essential to exit the crisis stronger and more united. the market turbulence of last week reminded us of the need to stay the course with reforms, in order to secure the confidence of the markets and, in doing so, unlock our growth potential and open up more job opportunities. this continues to be at the very core of the eu’s agenda going forward. there is clearly room for improvement. the next commission will review the europe 2020 strategy and will present the upcoming annual growth survey at the launch of the next european semester cycle. in the report there is, quite rightly, a great focus on the importance of implementing and monitoring the recommendations in the european semester. the recommendations must be concrete. they must not only address fiscal consolidation, but also structural reforms that can create sustainable and socially-balanced growth. jobs are making the eu market more competitive. the success of the european semester depends on implementation. this is why we monitor the implementation of reforms throughout the year and take action in case of insufficient or harmful policy development. it is important to recall that non-compliance with recommendations will not in itself trigger sanctions, but nor is it meant to. this is about policy coordination. implementation of the country-specific recommendations ultimately relies on national policy-making at the national parliaments. in this regard, i wish to take the opportunity to emphasise three significant findings in the report. first is the importance of putting in place a comprehensive mechanism that promotes the exchange of best practices between all national and eu-level actors responsible for getting more young people into work. in this regard, it is essential to speed up the implementation of programmes such as cosme, erasmus+ and horizon 2020, with nearly eur 80 billion of funding available over seven years. the second point is to devote more attention to improving the quality of jobs in order to match peoples’ skills with the real needs of the labour market. finally, i strongly support our fight against tax fraud and tax evasion and to shift the tax burden away from labour towards other forms of taxation that are less detrimental to growth and employment. one such example is environmental taxation. i see much agreement between the report and the commission’s own position. i hope this will be highlighted in our constructive and fruitful debate today.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the social partners are able to take part in the negotiations. - mr president, commissioner, this is the third year in a row that i have been involved in this debate and it is true that we have good reports resulting from the consensus, but do you know what is really sad? it's that today i could do exactly the same intervention that i did a year ago, two years ago and three years ago. i would like to repeat that too much austerity is still suffocating us economically in the european union and is still causing the highest unemployment rates in our history. i could say again that the strategy of savage wage devaluation that we are applying to gain competitiveness is making us more dependent on economic conditions outside, but it is also impoverishing us inside. i could tell you again that after the lavish public money we have spent to bail out the banks, credit still does not reach businesses and families, and that what does reach them is very high rates, precisely because we never demand economic credit counterparts to give that money. i could tell you that some of the structural reforms we have promoted, although necessary - labour, health, pensions - have depressed our domestic demand and multiplied inequality among europeans. i could say again that monetary policy alone will not get us out of the crisis, that we need to be brave with fiscal policy, with stimulus, with investment. it is a shame that we have only allocated six billion euros to combat youth unemployment, but what a shame that the states have not yet used them, and that those who are planning to do so are using them only to promote precariousness. i could tell you all this again. but, on the eve of the third recession in the european union, on the eve of the highest unemployment and poverty rates in our history, i can only think of one question to ask you, commissioner, and to the council: what the hell are you waiting for to change and to rectify?
mr president, commissioner, minister, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on the great work he has done in trying to agree on a common position. i agree with the rapporteur, with mr de backer, that we need to boost growth and job creation. but let us not be mistaken: sustainable growth will not be possible with a juncker plan alone, however ambitious it may be; it will not be possible to achieve sustainable growth with strong action by the european central bank, however ambitious it may be. to have sustainable growth, we need the joint action of all the actors involved: european institutions and member states; we need reforms: reforms in the member states and reforms in europe too. spain is a benchmark: it is one of the most ambitious countries in terms of reforms, and it is one of the countries with the highest growth in the eurozone and the most jobs being created. and we also need expansive tax policies in those countries that can afford it. we therefore need joint action by europe and the member states to consolidate and achieve sustainable growth.
mr president, despite some criticisms which we appreciate in the report, we cannot support it, especially paragraphs 5, 6 and, in particular, 8, which stress the importance of maintaining the process of structural reforms. we know that behind this expression we could have elements of positive change towards a more just, sustainable and equitable society, but the reality is just the opposite: 'structural reforms' is the euphemism that has been used to weaken public pension systems, to give more market share to private systems, much less sustainable. structural reforms in the labour market have meant that dismissals have become cheaper, collective bargaining has been boosted, wages have been reduced, often to the point of misery, and in return, for example in spain, there are now 400 000 fewer people in employment than before 2012, and this can be extended to many other countries. the semester is now the lever used to force internal devaluation and this parliament should be firm in condemning this type of process.
mr president, i will not analyse the time lost under the ideological paradigm of austerity over the last few years. i would like to focus, however, on this new discourse which is beginning to emerge in europe - as my colleague mr gualtieri has already mentioned - and which is included in this report on the european semester thanks to the amendments tabled by our group. i therefore call on the european commission, the new european commission, which will include commissioner katainen, to promote the europeanisation of economic policy in the euro area, banking union, capital market union and fiscal union. and i also believe, as mr balz does, that europe needs to have a greater capacity to implement the country-specific recommendations. and i think the new commission will have to redirect the tensions between france, italy and germany, because it is so complicated when a country does not follow the rules we have set ourselves, as when it has a current account surplus of more than 7% or 8% of gdp and the european commission does nothing. we therefore believe that this european semester is a step forward from the vision of the 'euro pattern' that we have suffered in recent years to a genuine economic union, and we believe that the new commission must lead it with a clear commitment.
mr president, commissioner, today we can see that, thanks to an improvement in the economic situation - especially in countries like mine which have made the necessary structural reforms - country-specific recommendations can be more focused on social issues and on what is fundamental. our objectives can be growth and job creation focused on innovative sectors such as ict, the green sector or the digital economy, and also poverty reduction. the european union is talking about economic, social and territorial cohesion, and to achieve this we must, on the one hand, pay greater attention to the most vulnerable groups and those furthest from the labour market through active employment policies aimed at improving education and employability and facilitating retraining and transition to employment, mainly through dual training and lifelong learning. and on the other hand, productive investments and improved interconnections with rural areas and areas with permanent natural or demographic difficulties are needed, as these tend to have higher unemployment rates and higher costs for access to public services such as education and health. finally, i would like to stress the importance of smes taking back the leading role in the european union.
