in writing. - on 19 november 2013, the european data protection supervisor delivered his opinion on the agreement between canada and the european union on the processing and transfer of passenger name record data. in that opinion, it questioned the necessity and proportionality of pnr schemes and of large-scale transfers of pnr data to third countries, as well as the choice of legal basis. i voted in favour of this report as it asks the court of justice for an opinion on the compatibility of the agreement with the treaties, as there is legal uncertainty as to the compatibility of the draft agreement with the provisions of the treaties (article 16) and of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union (articles 7, 8 and 52 (1)) as regards the right of individuals to the protection of their personal data. it also questions the choice of the legal basis, namely article 82 (1) (d) and article 87 (2) (a) tfeu (police and judicial cooperation) instead of article 16 tfeu (data protection).
in writing. - i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution because, as the aim of the agreement is to establish the conditions under which passenger name record (pnr) data may be transferred and used by the cbsa and to establish the way in which the data is protected, there is legal uncertainty as to its compatibility with certain articles of the eu treaty and the eu charter of fundamental rights. i therefore think it appropriate to ask the court of justice for an opinion on the compatibility of the agreement with the treaties.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this resolution to ask the court of justice of the european union to rule on the compatibility with the treaties and the charter of fundamental rights of the agreement between canada and the european union on the processing and transfer of passenger name record data. the judgment of the court of justice of 8 april 2014 declaring the data retention directive invalid raises legal uncertainties as to the compatibility of the draft agreement with the provisions of the treaties (article 16) and of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union (articles 7 and 8 and article 52 (1)), and it is therefore appropriate to request an opinion of the court of justice of the european union on this matter in order to ensure respect for the right of individuals to the protection of their personal data.

in writing. - the objective of this report is to contribute to shaping the eu's position at the next un conference in september 2015. it is the latest in a series of annual analyses by the ep on how the millennium development goals have worked, how to improve them and how to make them more viable. in recent years, the world has cut extreme poverty in half, and the fight against malaria and tuberculosis has produced dramatic results. but with the aim of a new post-2015 agreement, the international community is engaged in a broad process of analysis for a regulatory framework for global development. among our main contributions i would like to highlight the objective of eradicating extreme poverty, linking development and humanitarian aid, ensuring action in failed states, fighting tax evasion and corruption, looking after the specific needs of people with disabilities and showing greater strength on health and sexual and reproductive rights, minority rights and the rights of vulnerable people.
in writing. - in 2000, the united nations adopted the millennium declaration, with targets for 2015 that have reduced extreme poverty in the world by half or combat malaria and tuberculosis in a very important way. it is now necessary to promote and support a new post-2015 framework that includes the sustainability and growth goals of the international community, guided by the united nations. the ep is discussing how to contribute to the eu position to be defended in new york at the september 2015 summit. our main contributions include:- the identified goals and objectives must continue to revolve around the same main objective: eradicating poverty and inequality;- strong language on sexual and reproductive health and rights, on the rights of minorities and vulnerable people;- the fight against tax evasion and corruption. innovative sources of funding, such as the financial transaction tax;- the objective of meeting the specific needs of people with disabilities.

in writing. the eu is experiencing an unprecedented social emergency. since 2010, the number of people at risk of poverty and social exclusion has increased by 10 million to over 120 million. there are also almost 25 million unemployed in the eu-28 and many of those who do have a job do not make ends meet. that is why i voted in favour of the establishment of a minimum income for integration at european level: because i believe that the eu has a legal and moral obligation to ensure that europeans have sufficient income to cover their most basic needs. i also voted in favour of this resolution because i believe that there must be a change in the european semester policies to bring them into line with the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy, putting macroeconomic and employment and social priorities on the same level and ensuring that the jobs created in europe are of quality and with job guarantees. i believe we must increase investment in the fight against unemployment, poverty and social exclusion to put europe back on the path to smart, sustainable and inclusive growth.

in writing. while it is true that the content of most of the points in the resolution is clearly critical to take the gender perspective into account in employment material, to argue that social aspects should be of equal importance to macroeconomic ones or that improving the economy will not necessarily lead to more quality jobs, but that improving the quality of employment has to come from policies that are committed to it, we had to vote away, as other points in the resolution underline things that, in our opinion, are intolerable. they stress that the problem of youth unemployment is due to young people not being sufficiently trained, not having leadership skills or not being entrepreneurial; that the mobility of workers must be encouraged and the labour market made even more flexible. these measures only throw the ball away, blaming young people for not having jobs, forcing workers to go into exile to find work and encouraging the precariousness of employment with more and more flexibility which, in countries like spain, we know leads to a further deterioration of the labour market.
in writing. - if we are to achieve the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy and eliminate the situations of dependence of people with disabilities, it is crucial that equality be guaranteed in all areas of community policy and, in particular, in access to the labour market for people with disabilities. in this regard, the measures provided for in the united nations convention on the rights of persons with disabilities and the reports elaborating on it should be adopted. as the case law of the court of justice of the eu has shown, the convention is the first legally binding international human rights instrument to which the european union has become a party. the european union is therefore bound by the convention within the limits of its competence, and the employment equality directive, as far as possible, should be interpreted in a manner consistent with the convention.

the rapporteur. - madam president, mr zanetti, the truth is that i have been thinking for several days about what i am going to say here today. i have been reviewing all the meetings we have had with the council, with the italian presidency, with the commission and i have been compiling all the arguments we have put on the table to defend the european parliament's proposal. because i think it's a proposal that is very easy to understand: we have to pay what we owe. the european union cannot have debts. the european union cannot be lax with its citizens, its organisations, its town halls or its students. and to defend this proposal, which is so easy, we have given them legal arguments, because article 310 of the tfeu says that the budget of the european union must be in balance. we have given them economic reasons, because it is not understandable that we should ask our states to pay their debts and we should increase ours. we have given them reasons for doing so, because it is unacceptable that we owe more than 25 billion euros in cohesion funds to the countries that are suffering the most and need it the most. solidarity reasons, and commissioner georgieva knows this very well: we cannot accept that our ngos in the field of humanitarian aid have no money to carry out their programmes. and even opportunity reasons, because we have five billion extra euros in revenue, which can help to alleviate the situation. but all these reasons have clearly not worked. thomas paine once said that 'time converts more than reason', and i think that is a perfect description of what has happened at the european council. because over time they will move up in positions, over time they will understand that we have a problem of non-payment, and over time they will understand that the multiannual financial framework, even if only partially, has parts of flexibility. we had 21 days to reach an agreement and it was not possible; so we are giving them extra time to see if we have any more converts within the council. i said earlier that when i was preparing this speech i was gathering all the arguments, but i was also trying to think of any new idea, any magic phrase, any keyword that could get the council out of that hypnosis that seems to blind them to reality. and the magic word was said to me today by mr renzi at a meeting we had: politics. that is what we need, because it is politics that will enable us to get out of this rigidity which we have today in the council. because politics is what will allow us to move forward on agreements and get out of this deadlock. the european parliament is prepared to put all policies and all proposals on the table, but we need receptivity on the part of the council. and if the council wants to make proposals to solve the problem of non-payment, we will accept them, because all we want is to be able to pay people, to be able to pay for projects and for the european project to go ahead.
madam president, the union's budgets are meager and unsocial, but they are redistributive, as things are. the richer countries contribute more and the countries with problems receive proportionately more investment. this solidarity between peoples, however small, means much more than trade union. it makes us friends and brothers, not just partners. but it also makes us stronger. an unequal europe is certainly an unjust and sad europe, but it is also a poor and fragile europe. that is why it is not only selfish and unsolidarist, but also short-sighted and irresponsible for the northern governments to try to increase the social gap, together with the union's debt, by 4 000 million. let them not then accuse the countries of the south of wanting to leave europe. the eurosceptics are them.

member of the commission. - madam president, i would like to thank the members, and the members of the committee on women’s rights and gender equality in particular, for the opportunity to answer the questions relating to this very serious subject. it is an important symbol that the debate is taking place today on 25 november: the international day for the elimination of violence against women. i hope that in one year’s time i will be allowed here to speak about better results and a better situation in the field we are going to speak about. violence against women remains one of the most serious human rights violations of our time. it is deeply rooted in gender inequalities and reinforces them. it is an extreme form of discrimination. one in three women in the european union has experienced physical or sexual violence since the age of fifteen. i was myself shocked by reading the latest figures given by the fundamental rights agency in vienna. i did not know myself that the situation is that bad in the european union. i would like to stress in this place that for me, this problem is not a matter of statistics, because this concerns any individual. we had the pope here today. he spoke about human dignity. this is what is at stake in this problem, in this field: not only human dignity but lives themselves, as you have said. violence against women affects society as a whole and is also costly. parliament’s european added-value assessment estimated the direct cost of violence against women in the european union at eur 69 billion per year. it suggests that if we reduce violence by just 10%, the direct economic costs would be reduced by approximately eur 7 billion a year. tackling violence against women therefore makes economic sense too, but again i want to stress that i understand this problem as more than an economic problem, for sure. this is just an illustration of economic figures. i can assure you that i share your commitment to eliminating violence against women. this will be reflected in the new commission strategy for equality between women and men, in which there will be a chapter on gender-based violence. this strategy has been proposed by my services and by myself to be elaborated for the year 2015, and i am inviting a wide discussion on this topic under the preparatory work for this strategy. violence against women is a complex phenomenon and there is no magic wand which makes it disappear at once. if we really want to make a lasting difference then i believe that we have to address it as part of our greater common struggle for equality. our action must therefore be steady, coherent and based on several pillars. these are: legislation, awareness-raising and funding, as well as improving knowledge and data collection. allow me now to go through these instruments we have in hand. as regards legislation: the eu has put in place a coherent legal framework to prevent all forms of violence against women and to support victims. this framework now includes the equal treatment directive and its provisions on sexual harassment, the directive on trafficking in human beings, the directive against sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, the directive on the european protection order applicable in criminal matters, the regulation setting the european protection order (covering civil matters), and last but not least, the directive on the rights of crime victims, which emphasises the need for tailored protection and support for victims of gender-based violence. the commission is now guiding and monitoring member states in the effective implementation of this legal framework. so this is the list of existing legislation, and the expression of the necessity to adopt new legislation may be one of the results of working on the new strategy on equality between men and women which we are going to prepare next year. prevention measures and the cross-border dimension of gender-based violence that you have raised in your question are addressed by the istanbul convention of the council of europe. insofar as the eu has competence to sign and ratify the convention, i believe we should consider eu accession to it. it is equally important that member states respect their commitments and ratify this convention as soon as possible. to date, and over four years after the adoption of the convention, 22 eu member states have signed it, but only eight eu member states have ratified it so far. so i ask all of those here who are from member states which have not ratified the convention to go to their governments, their national parliaments and their media and call for national ratifications of the first international legally binding instrument combating violence against women. the second pillar of what we can – and what we must – do is awareness-raising and funding. the second pillar of the commission’s approach to combating violence against women involves supporting awareness-raising and grassroots actions by member states, civil society organisations and european networks. for example, this year eur 9.5 million were allocated to supporting european networks and grassroots projects to combat violence against women under the rights, equality and citizenship programme. our objective is to make a real difference in women’s and girls’ lives, also by the good use of this supporting money. the commission will monitor and evaluate the ongoing awareness-raising and prevention efforts before deciding on possible future awareness-raising activities such as a european year to end violence against women. improving our knowledge of the prevalence and causes of gender-based violence is essential, because it allows the situation to be monitored across the eu and holds governments and stakeholders accountable. it also helps us to formulate and implement better policies, beyond a mere benchmarking exercise. comparable eu data shows us how to improve the prevention of violence and the protection of victims. we can learn from each other, from our successes and failures. my services are working with eurostat and the european institute for gender equality, two key actors in the area which i believe can help fill these gaps. as a follow-up to the directive on the rights of crime victims, eurostat, in cooperation with national statistical offices, started in 2014 to collect more detailed crime data recorded by the police and justice systems. the results, disaggregated by sex, will be published in 2015 and will constitute a step forward in our efforts to better understand gender-based violence. however, to complement police records, comprehensive and in-depth surveys are necessary. the already-mentioned fundamental rights agency survey paved the way in this field. it is now considered the gold standard, and we should be proud of this achievement. however, we cannot stop here and now. we need to repeat the fundamental rights agency survey again, and we will make sure that such surveys are conducted at regular intervals to detect new trends and gaps. in my view we need to use existing tools more effectively rather than establishing new bodies like the european observatory on violence against women. instead, we need an orchestrated effort from all relevant bodies, making full use of the existing expertise. as you know, the commission will adopt a new strategy on equality between women and men from 2015. gender-based violence will be a priority of this strategy. i am committed to addressing new forms of violence emerging in an increasingly connected world, such as cyber violence and harassment. while new means of communication and technology offer great opportunities in combating violence against women, they can pose a new threat to the security of women as well. the most effective course of action will be determined and integrated in the new commission strategy on equality between women and men. this strategy must also include actions to engage men in combating violence against women, raising their awareness of the issue but also engaging them as actors for change. only by working together will our efforts be fully effective. finally, i would like to engage with you and listen to you and other stakeholders when developing this new strategy.

on behalf of the alde group. madam president, commissioner jourová, we are shocked to learn that one in three women in the world - and yes, european women too - will suffer sexual, physical or psychological violence at some point in their lives simply because they are women. however, the reality is far worse than the shocking figures we know, because only a third of the victims report it. the question is, again, what can we do? i am going to propose to you here and now, and i am also going to propose to you, that we do something immediately, radically concrete, revolutionarily effective: ratify the istanbul convention. it is the first integrated and legally binding document that establishes that violence against women and domestic violence is a serious attack on human rights. the istanbul convention is a unique instrument, committing each state that ratifies it to detect, prevent and eliminate violence against girls and women in all its manifestations, from domestic abuse to forced marriage, female genital mutilation or trafficking for exploitation. a comprehensive legal tool already exists which requires the protection of victims, the adoption of legislative and punitive measures against perpetrators and the development of effective equality policies. it's in effect since august 1st, it's ready and at our disposal. what are we waiting for to adopt him? to date, only eight member states have ratified the istanbul convention: spain, portugal, italy, france, sweden, denmark, austria and malta. fourteen have already signed and are in the process of ratifying. but today is a good day to ask bulgaria, estonia, ireland, the czech republic, cyprus and latvia why they have not even signed it yet. today is a good day for this parliament to call unequivocally on the commission to accept this mandate and on the new latvian presidency to take a firm lead in this indispensable process from january onwards. as a reference point in the defence of democracy and human rights in the world, it is essential that europe has a unanimous voice; unanimous in rejecting, persecuting and punishing violence against women; unanimous in the quality public debate that explicitly and decisively incorporates men, such as dr mukwege, for example; and unanimous in promoting and implementing political and legislative measures that end the inequality that persists and that we are ashamed of, the inequality that is at the root of violence against women. president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you to all who have spoken. it was an interesting debate, not new in many respects, but it is very important that it should take place at the beginning of this parliamentary term. it is clear, as has been said and as i said in my introduction, that in this political cycle europe is either making a difference on issues such as immigration or it will have a very hard time regaining credibility in the eyes of its citizens. immigration is just one of the test cases on which we will have to see how much europe can do together. and the most integrated approach is certainly an approach which starts from the external dimension which links - as several of you have said and as the council we fully share this - development policies and security policies. it is clear that there is a direct link with the contribution that the european union as such (although we are the world's leading donor) can make to the fight against poverty. it is also true that there is a security aspect, starting with border security. i would remind you that, on the initiative of the presidency, the council set itself the medium-term objective work on in the new legislature. it is clear, and we have also mentioned this in the council's discussions, that much more cooperation is needed between the european union and countries of origin and transit. in particular, i would like to add to the debate the commitment that the council has made to work much more effectively and much more intensively on voluntary resettlement programmes, on initiatives in regions bordering on crisis regions outside the european union, together with the united nations high commissioner for refugees. it is an operational commitment which was made in the luxembourg council of ministers of the interior, and on which the council and parliament will certainly have to work much more closely together. the question of rescuing people at sea was also raised. i would remind you that the duty to assist people in distress at sea is part of international law. it is binding on all member states, it is binding on all those involved, including in the mediterranean, and it is binding on rescuers regardless of their nationality and, i would stress this, regardless of the status of the people to be rescued. it's not that if a person is an illegal immigrant, we can drown them, but if they're an economic immigrant or a potential asylum seeker, we can save them. this is a very important point to stress. obviously, then, this duty to assist people in difficulty, which is binding on the member states, also applies to operations with frontex's contribution, such as operation triton. of course, operation triton is the beginning of a shared response, it is the beginning of a shared responsibility, it is a good starting point, around which we have to build a lot more. of course we need more funding, starting with frontex. but certainly funds without new common policies cannot suffice. it is very important that in the strategic agenda for the new legislature the european council has identified the commitment to fully develop common legal and illegal immigration policies, but for this - i repeat again - trust and solidarity are needed. and if we do not rebuild within the european union a relationship of trust and solidarity between us, much of this and much of what you have also wished for will remain on paper. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. some countries complain that there are a disproportionate number of asylum seekers on their territory. other countries are complaining about uncontrolled, sometimes uncontrollable, mass arrivals of illegal immigrants on their shores. and it seems that sometimes there is a competition as to who has more rights or who has more need of common intervention. but it is clear that it is precisely the absence of a common policy, whether on legal immigration or on illegal immigration, that is imposing a disproportionate cost both on countries with very high numbers of asylum seekers and on countries whose coasts are exposed to massive irregular inflows. it is clear that in both cases the answer can be a new common european policy on legal and illegal immigration. it's not that we can continue to play the game of need, which also means the game of a lack of trust between us. it is a policy to be built up step by step, proposal by proposal. a new directive on access to the european union for research, study and voluntary work is currently being negotiated between the council of ministers and the european parliament. another piece of that common legal immigration policy which we must absolutely build, because it is obvious that all this will be built over the course of a whole parliamentary term, step by step, piece by piece. the commissioner in his opening speech referred to the commission's possible proposal for better distribution and burden-sharing. that is certainly another very important point. as regards unaccompanied foreign minors, i indicated in my introduction that we must first of all make use of all the possibilities that the existing dublin rules on unaccompanied minors allow, which have not been exploited and on which we must work, and i recall that some member states are working on legislative proposals to this end. i agree with him completely and this is one of the subjects we have also discussed in the council. it is impossible, mr president, to answer all the speeches. but surely we will either really have the courage and the will to have a common approach or we will lose everything and also lose the credibility of the european union in relation to our citizens.

access to the asylum procedures. i want to be clear on that. any border surveillance measure must be proportionate to the objectives pursued. it must be in compliance with respect for the eu charter on fundamental rights and the principle, as i mentioned before, of non-refoulement, and it must respect human dignity. in accordance with these obligations, border control must be carried out while respecting the rights of refugees and persons requesting international protection, in particular as regards the principle of non-refoulement and effective access to the asylum procedures. any cooperation with third countries must be carried out in full respect of these principles. it is necessary to guarantee effective access to the asylum procedure for those third-country nationals who are on member state territory, including at the borders, in transit zones or on the territorial seas, and who express a wish to apply for asylum. the commission is also concerned that the interpretation by spain of what constitutes an external border, and recent proposals amending relevant legislation – what some have called ‘hot returns’ – might not be in conformity with obligations arising under eu and international law. my predecessor, commissioner malmström, had requested that the spanish minister of the interior provide the commission with information concerning these draft amendments. in addition, my services have already addressed the spanish authorities at the technical level to better understand the implications of these draft amendments and their conformity with spain’s obligations under european union law. as guardian of the treaties, the commission follows closely the actions of member states, and it is the responsibility of the commission to draw attention to actions which may constitute a violation of european union laws, in particular when it concerns the protection of the fundamental rights of individuals. the commission will not hesitate to take appropriate steps where there is evidence that a member state has violated european union laws. but i am confident that the dialogue we have opened with the spanish authorities will have positive results and will lead to the necessary changes, and i am planning to accept the invitation of the minister and confirm, together with him, the improvements in such a difficult part of our common the answer is 'blue card'. the answer is very simple. every time a member state breaches european law, the commission intervenes, and for that purpose it is the guardian of the treaties. and it is being debated in this european parliament. but you know what i'm saying? that is not only contrary to european law, it is also contrary to spanish legislation, which does not allow for 'hot returns'. spanish legislation provides for expulsions, in accordance with a regulated procedure and with a sanctioning character, which is not the case of a person illegally intercepted. spanish legislation also provides for refusal at the border, but at the points where this is possible and in accordance with a regulated procedure, but in no case does it provide for direct surrender to the moroccan authorities, which would mean ignoring or violating the procedure regulated by spanish law and which offers no guarantee, either of legal assistance, information on your rights or of an interpreter. that is contrary, first of all, to spanish law, but it is also contrary to european law and to refugee protection law, in that it does not give any chance to the percentage, however small, of those who are fleeing persecution or who deserve subsidiary protection to prove that they are in a situation which deserves protection by a member state of the european union.

in writing. for people with disabilities, insufficient access to the labour market can mean that they are in socially vulnerable situations and exposed to serious risks of discrimination, poverty and social exclusion. in eu countries, 49% of women with disabilities and 61% of men with disabilities are in employment, compared with 64% of women without disabilities and 89% of men. the terrible consequence of all this is that the poverty rate for disabled people is 70% higher than the average, due to limited access to employment. in the light of these data, special attention is needed to eliminate, or at least reduce, employment inequality in the field of disability, and to adopt so-called 'reasonable adjustments'. in this connection, the eu has proclaimed in various provisions that compliance with the principle of equal treatment in relation to persons with disabilities implies the adoption of reasonable accommodation. this means that employers will take appropriate measures, depending on the needs of each specific situation, to enable disabled people to access, take part in or progress in employment.
member of the commission. - mr president, i think, from the comments we have heard, there is a broad welcome for the stress test but a clear feeling that the job is not yet done, and that is a conclusion that i would share. i think in terms of the credibility of the test, which is one of the themes of the debate, i would argue that the exercise was credible because a robust methodology was followed; there was a great deal of detail in the quality assurance; there was strong governance and multiple layers of accountability. i think, since, that investors and analysts have praised the degree of disclosure and the degree of transparency about how the tests were run, and i think that there has also been a broadly positive market reaction, since the results were announced a month ago, and i believe that is testament to the credibility of the exercise. one of the points that was raised repeatedly – in slightly different ways – was the question of whether this is enough and whether it will lead to the pickup in bank lending that we all want to see. the purpose of the exercise was to identify and address vulnerabilities in the banking system and to try and dispel some of those doubts about its health – but it was not an exercise for its own sake; rather, the purpose was to try to restore investor trust and confidence. i believe that the european banking authority and the ecb did an excellent job and that they have successfully met the objectives of the exercise. we have devoted a lot of attention to the supply side, but in order to get lending going again, we need the demand side to pick up as well, and that is also something we need to look at. our foremost priority at the commission is to create an environment conducive to growth so that businesses can create jobs and our economies can prosper once more. that, of course, is the background to the investment initiative, which president juncker will be announcing to parliament tomorrow; and it is also the prism through which i intend to look at the question of regulation and regulation of the banking sector. i believe that a healthy european banking sector is one that supports growth and benefits eu citizens, businesses and society as a whole. it is a system, as a number of colleagues said, where taxpayers are no longer exposed to the risk of bank failures; it is a system that is solid; it is a system that is stable, without banks which are too big to fail, too costly to save or too complex to resolve. that means it needs to be a system that is responsibly regulated, managed and supervised, based on strong ethical standards and sound governance. ms ferreira reminded us of the need for the next steps on banking union, and i agree with what she said about that. an important task has been started, but there is more work to do, and she reminded us of some of the immediate steps that i know she and her colleagues are working on at the moment. i also take the point that we need to be alert to new risks and to look, as i said, in particular at the question of ‘too big to fail’. but i believe – although there is more work to do – that the results of the eu-wide stress tests have brought us one step nearer to a healthy banking system, and that the stress tests and the comprehensive assessment will help restore confidence in our banks. that will allow them to turn their attention to supporting growth for the benefit of us and the benefit of european citizens.
on 26 october the european central bank and the european banking authority published the results of the global analysis of the european banking system, comprising the review of the quality of banking assets (aqr) and the so-called stress tests, which analysed the solvency of 150 banking institutions in the eu countries and, in particular, in the euro area. first, these tests are based on a simulation exercise. in addition, the method of evaluation chosen by the european central bank is to ask the different banks to send it a balance sheet report, which leaves room for the banks to falsify the accounts. an example of the lack of neutrality in such tests occurred in 2010 when many irish and spanish entities, including bankia, passed the stress tests and had to receive public support shortly after passing the stress tests. therefore, we cannot consider that the stress tests on banks respond to reliable mechanisms. to ask us citizens who have paid the consequences of putting public money into private banks to trust such results is practically an act of faith.
in writing. it is not surprising that banks recover their solvency when citizens are forced to contribute to their rescue with all kinds of sacrifices. this is even less so when a tailor-made exercise is prepared, by softening, as in the case of spain, the macroeconomic forecasts or by omitting an analysis of the systematic interactions between banks and other unregulated parts of the financial system. if the purpose of the stress tests was to allow credit to flow, i warn you of their failure. without a restructuring of private debts, households and smes will remain more concerned with reducing their debt than with negotiating new loans: neither will companies invest while demand remains depressed, nor will households, punished by unemployment and low wages, think of taking out a mortgage. in spain too, banking was solvent and regulation exemplary; it happened that it was the economic system as a whole that could not resist its dependence on debt. when the bubble bursts, it can only be followed by stagnation. the return to growth requires a productive alternative to the financialisation they insist on imposing.

vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i would like to thank you all for your very valuable contribution. from now on, we have to concentrate on very deep cooperation in order to make this plan real. today, mr juncker’s commission is fulfilling the first promise we made when we were appointed: we are setting out an investment plan that will change the way public money is used for investment in europe. there is ample liquidity in the market. interest rates are very low and financial market tension has eased. at the same time, there is a real demand for credible investment projects, and yet investment is not happening. there is a severe disconnect. uncertainties and risk aversion are stifling investment flows. public authorities can play a vital role in both supply and demand. we need to make long-term financing available for projects that contribute towards our common priorities for europe: energy, digital, transport, and research and innovation. to succeed, europe must be united and innovative. we can only deliver a programme of this scale and ambition with the strong political support of this house. we count on your support for this investment plan, to sustain its high level of ambition and to send a clear message to voters that their voices have been heard. i know that attention will be concentrated today on the additional financial capacity. important as this is, for me this is not enough in itself. as i said in my hearing, i do not want to just put numbers on a piece of paper or money on a table. therefore, we are presenting a major reform of investment at european level. we want to make sure that real investment happens in the real economy and that we create real new opportunities in europe. the eu investment plan is a triangle, with three parts. firstly, we will ensure that every euro invested through this plan maximises its impact on the real economy. to achieve this, we will launch a european fund for strategic investment together with the eib. this fund will be underpinned by guarantees from the eu budget and a capital contribution from the eib worth a total of eur 21 billion. the new, fresh lending capacity of this new fund will be more than eur 60 billion to the real economy. it will be directed at higher-risk investments providing first-loss guarantees – and i want to repeat this: it will be directed at higher-risk investments providing first-loss guarantees – to complement the traditional lending activity of the eib. it will also be used to finance long-term strategic investment and to provide additional finance for smes and mid-sized companies. the fund, which is backed by a solid eu guarantee, will bring in more money from investors in the public and private sector, who will be reassured by a lower risk. we estimate that, by this multiplier effect, the fund will unlock public and private investment into the real economy to a value of more than eur 300 billion. this is a robust, conservative assumption based on previous eib and eu experiences. this is not about complex financial instruments for their own sake but about making investment happen. to those who claim that this is not ʽrealʼ money, my reply is: nonsense. this is a very real, additional public lending capacity of more than eur 60 billion which acts as a magnet to draw in real investment in real projects and create real jobs. what it is not is an expensive cash handout which will damage our public-sector finances and have no longer-term sustainable impact. today, we come together to deliver our part. the next step is for national governments to step in and provide additional capital to the fund, and we strongly encourage member states to do so. the member states’ contribution to the fund will be stability and growth pact (sgp)-neutral. in addition to this, we also look to the member states to use their eu structural funds better and to double the use of financial instruments such as loans and guarantees. currently, 92% of structural funds go to grant schemes. this has to change. once the money is granted, it is gone. we need to make better use of this financing so that it goes further and has a real effect on the economy. at the heart of this package there is a political choice: either we continue business as usual with traditional grants and loans and that is as far as the money goes, or we use our budget in the most efficient way to support riskier borrowing and create a larger lending capacity. this is the choice we have made. it is a new approach at european level, to change the way public money is used. as a second pillar, we want to make sure that this money reaches the real economy. together with the eib we are creating a transparent pipeline of trusted investment. we will be identifying viable projects at eu level and stepping up the necessary technical assistance to support project structuring and the use of more innovative financial instruments for member states. this is what investors are asking for. there is money out there, but investors tell us they need well-structured, high-quality projects with access to clear and transparent information. the task force led by the commission and the eib, with member states, is currently identifying over a thousand projects which are ready to be assessed. we want to give a european label for the most viable ones. we need sound investments for the future, not another bubble. that is why we are proposing this combination of guarantees at eu level for higher-risk investments, along with longer-term projects in line with our strategic priorities. together they will enable us to start moving quickly and also to deliver sustainable investment for the long term. thirdly, we want to remove barriers to investment by the private sector. we need to step up our efforts to have better regulation. we need to work with the member states to renew europe with structural reforms which create a more favourable investment environment and better competitiveness and create more growth and jobs. we want to create a single market in the energy, digital, capital, public procurement and services areas. this helps to remove regulatory barriers for business to invest. there are many companies out there creating digital products. they have a single market in the united states but not here. there are many people who want to invest in the energy sector, but until they have an energy union they cannot do so as easily as, say, in the food sector. the single market needs to be deepened in services and in public procurement. i will also support my fellow commissioners in completing the single market in energy, the digital sector and transport. i will also work closely with commissioner jonathan hill to deliver a capital markets union. we need a financial sector which serves our companies better – especially smes – and reduces their dependence on financing from the banks. for me, this single market dimension – the third side of the triangle – is the most important part of our work and the one that really changes europe permanently. of course, this will not happen overnight, but we can make change together if we are determined. this is our joint responsibility. each of these three strands of the investment triangle is needed to make investment happen in europe. each strand reinforces the others. i am sure some will say that the money of this new investment fund is not enough. we do not need – and we do not want – to maximise the taxpayers’ burden. what matters is real investment, not just large sums of money sitting in a bank. we are going to use a relatively small amount of public money to remove the fear factor and unlock the investment funds which are already there and waiting to be used. we need just enough money to get the motor running. after that it will have a life of its own. if member states still believe these funds are not enough, we invite them to make their own additional contributions. for the investment plan to succeed, member states must take courageous decisions and the ecb will need to play its part. on its own, the plan is not a magic bullet to transform the european economy but – and it is a very important but – if we implement all three elements of our plan, we will change the european investment landscape permanently and structurally for the better. so let us all get to work together to get investments working in europe again.
in writing. the €315 billion investment plan proposed by the commission is a first step towards stimulating growth in europe's depressed economy - a plan that has come under pressure from the socialist group in the european parliament. the design submitted contains uncertainties which should be clarified in the coming weeks. the fund starts with a small initial capital provided by the eib, the rest being guarantees based on the commission's budgets. the participation of the states through guarantees and through capital from countries with fiscal leeway is vital. the fund should also have a credible governance model that allows for a professionalised selection of projects, with a greater impact on economies with worse prospects. the credibility of new projects will be central to achieving the high level of private capital involvement on which the whole programme is based. we will work in the coming months in the european parliament to clarify the uncertainties of the juncker plan and to make it more ambitious, but also to make more changes in the hitherto misguided european economic policy.

in writing. the €315 billion investment plan proposed by the commission, following pressure from the s&d group, is good news for the depressed european economy. its urgent need is widely shared in academia, as shown by numerous economic studies, and by citizens, who have shaped social initiatives such as new deal 4 europe. the socialists welcome this step taken by the commission at the request of our group. the design submitted contains uncertainties which should be clarified in the coming weeks. the fund starts with a small initial capital provided by the eib, the rest being guarantees based on the commission's budgets. the participation of the states through guarantees and through capital from countries with fiscal leeway is vital. the fund should also have a credible governance model that allows for a professionalised selection of projects, with a greater impact on economies with worse prospects. the credibility of new projects will be central to achieving the high level of private capital involvement on which the whole programme is based.
in writing. the investment plan proposed by the president of the commission aims to mobilise €315 billion of public and private capital to revitalise the european economy and create jobs. the impact on gdp growth rate is expected to be between 2,5 and 3,1 per cent and the creation of 1,3 million new jobs in the period 2015-2017. although the commission proposal does not require contributions or guarantees from the states, it is worth noting that this has two positive aspects: the investment made by the programme will not count in the calculation of the deficit, and the governance of the new efsi will not adopt an intergovernmental structure, but will be under the aegis of the commission and the eib. the weakest aspects are the unrealistic proposed leverage of 1 to 15 and the lack of mention of the ecb's participation in the purchase of the bonds issued to finance the efsi.

on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, mr commissioner, kyoto was a great decision to ensure that the future of humanity is at risk from climate change. but the effects that should have been obtained by the full implementation of the kyoto protocol have been held back by two wrong decisions, by two wrong approaches: that of the developed countries, which have believed that to get out of the crisis one had to abandon the policies of sustainability and the fight against climate change, and that of the underdeveloped countries, which have come out, because they have believed that growth is not compatible with respect for the environment. yet during this time, the evidence of climate change has continued to grow. crises are becoming more frequent. lima must be the first step towards the great ambition of kyoto, and paris must be the consolidation of that ambition. there are positive signs. the european union has made commitments. it is true that parliament wanted more. more than the commission and the commission more than the council. but we made commitments. china and the united states are doing it. and the g77 is doing it. it is time for these commitments to be precise objectives, concrete actions, new financing, support and solidarity for developing countries. lima must be the place to prepare the recovery of a great ambition that, to a certain extent, has been lost along the way.
mr president, we need to develop an ecologically sustainable economic model, which, in my view, means laying the foundations for a real and credible transition to an ecological economic model, as a means, of course, to achieve real progress that is inclusive of all people, and i am certainly not talking only at european level. when we talk about fighting climate change, we are talking about transforming the current model; we are talking about social, economic and environmental justice, that is, an alternative model very different from the current one, a model that must integrate, in turn, mobility and energy policies with public planning, policies of spatial planning, consumption and production processes, waste management, a new model of taxation on environmental bases. we are talking about fundamentally changing the economic cycle. as merja kyllönen has pointed out, we need a comprehensive action plan and more ambitious steps.
mr president, the european union is presenting itself as a leader at the climate change summit, but the reality is starting to be less accurate. for example, in spain there has been an increase in emissions of 5.2 per cent for the electricity generation sector, even during the crisis, according to data from the national institute of statistics. we still have an economy addicted to oil and coal. the european union continues to support electricity companies, which use the most expensive and polluting energy sources - such as coal and gas - and increase the cost of electricity while increasing energy poverty. out of the picture are emissions imported from international trade, including the failed european emissions trading system, hot air purchases, etc. if we take the european union as a whole, the carbon footprint increases by 25 percent when we include imports. the allocation of emission allowances is scandalous. the most polluting ones have been 'fed' at the expense of emissions trading and their use has become a source of surplus for the companies themselves. is it not time to start thinking that the solutions are through binding laws and not so much through money, money and money?
mr president, commissioner, we in the european union have made countless efforts to combat climate change, both in the conferences of the parties and in our internal policies. and that we're only responsible for 11% of emissions. we are on track to meet our commitment to reduce emissions by 20% by 2020 and this is thanks to research, new technologies, the promotion of renewable energy, new standards for car emissions and the replacement of energy sources by less polluting ones. we have the best guarantee for a new international negotiation in which the european union must not only make offers to its partners, but must also make demands. because meeting our 2020 target comes at a cost that is being borne by families and businesses. we need an international agreement to unify the environmental conditions under which industrial activity, agriculture, energy generation and transport take place around the world. european citizens and businesses cannot continue to bear the cost of fighting climate change. the commission and the member states must use all the resources available to achieve a balanced agreement by next year, in which everyone is equally committed to the fight against climate change, as the european union is committing itself.
mr president, it is not the fight against climate change that is the burden of the citizens in terms of costs. it is the change in policies of some governments, as is the case of spain, which has stopped betting on renewable energies and that has been a blow to those families who had invested in it. but let's talk about the lima conference. amendment no 9 by the european people's party breaks with a traditional ambition of this parliament. it is a step backwards that they want to impose on us, by removing the binding targets on efficiency and renewables. it is a sign of what this legislature has in store for us. it is a nod to certain interests that are supported by some countries. and i would like to know whether this is also the position of the european commission. today you want us to give up the demand for binding targets. they say in their amendment that what happens is that there are different views on the role we should play. don't get us confused this parliament has always had a vocation to fight climate change and we cannot take a step back.
in writing. i voted against this report which approves the draft contained in the recommendation of the european central bank as amended in relation to the collection of statistical information by the european central bank, as one of the new powers conferred on this body. from the outset, my group has criticised most elements of banking union, including those relating to increasing the power of the ecb. that is why i voted against.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the draft regulation because i share the ecb's recommendation that regulation (ec) no 2533/1998 be amended to adapt it to the ecb's new supervisory tasks in accordance with regulation (eu) no 1024/2013. these changes will allow it to use confidential statistical information to fulfil its supervisory role. furthermore, it shall be permitted to transmit this information to the european system of central banks, the authorities and bodies of the member states and of the union responsible for supervision for the exercise of their respective functions.
in writing. - the financial crisis has highlighted the need to improve regulation and supervision of the financial sector in the eu, which is why i voted in favour of the ecb being able to use confidential statistical information for the performance of its new supervisory functions and for its transmission within the european system of central banks to national and eu authorities and bodies responsible for the supervision and stability of financial institutions, markets and infrastructures under the european stability mechanism and the legislation in force. we compensate for this by requiring the authorities receiving the information to take all the necessary regulatory, administrative, technical and organisational measures to ensure the physical and computer protection of its confidentiality.
in writing. i voted against this report which approves the draft contained in the recommendation of the european central bank as amended in relation to the collection of statistical information by the european central bank, as one of the new powers conferred on this body. from the outset, my group has criticised most elements of banking union, including those relating to increasing the power of the ecb. that is why i voted against.
in writing. we voted against the report because it is part of the new banking union they want to establish by giving the ecb more power. the fact that the ecb is responsible for monitoring and at the same time dictating the monetary policy of the countries of the european union creates a conflict of interest which we must bear in mind when analysing what the establishment of a european banking union will entail. because at a certain point monetary policy decisions (such as interest rate movements) may conflict with the objective of financial stability. thus, if monitoring detects a stability problem, the solution may require a change in interest rates in the opposite direction.
in writing. - i have supported the proposal to amend regulation (ec) no 2533/98 on the collection of statistics by the european central bank (ecb) as the econ committee has succeeded in substantially improving this rule, thanks in part to amendments put forward by my group, the socialists and democrats, including some of my own contributions. the ecb has therefore achieved a more transparent, coherent and internally consistent rule, which has required going beyond the articles that the ecb recommended to be amended. at least three improvements are worth noting. first, any exemption from the obligation to provide statistics will have to be justified and made public. secondly, a distinction is made between incorrect and manipulated statistical information, which will allow the possible sanctions to be graded. third, the ecb's inspection work is strengthened by granting it the power to access the raw data of the entities subject to the statistical reporting obligation. however, it should be borne in mind that a majority was not reached in favour of updating the level of the sanctions, which are not entirely proportionate to the various types of conduct and are hardly dissuasive.

in writing. - i have supported this report in an attempt to make this regulation more consistent and coherent. progress has been made in differentiating between incorrect and manipulated information and, for sanctions purposes, it has been clarified that the ecb has the power to request raw data from financial institutions, as well as the need to justify in writing any exemption from entities providing statistical information. however, the fines, which date back to 1998 and are now out of date, have not been updated.

in writing. the adoption of the single supervisory mechanism requires an amendment to council regulation (ec) no 2532/98. in particular, article 18 of the ssm gives the ecb new powers to impose administrative pecuniary sanctions when banks breach directly applicable union law. from the outset my group has criticised most elements of banking union, including those relating to an increase in the power of the ecb. the ecb should not be given any more powers than it already has. that is why i voted against.
in writing. - i voted in favour because, as a consequence of the adoption of council regulation (eu) no 1024/2013 of 15 october 2013, the ecb has competence for the prudential supervision of credit institutions. this requires the definition of periodic budgets, the general budgets and the scope of application, the penalties for non-compliance, the procedure for initiating infringement proceedings and the time limits for penalties.
in writing. - the crisis has required the adoption of rules to ensure that financial agents, products and markets are properly regulated and effectively supervised, with banking union as the backbone, for the long-term survival and prosperity of the euro. comprehensive supervision was needed, hence the recent launch of the single supervisory mechanism for the euro area, now with the ecb as the ultimate supervisor tasked with ensuring a consistent and coherent application of the single rulebook and able to decide to directly supervise any credit institution. beyond transparency on the quality of bank assets, the ecb needed clear and unequivocal authority to impose sanctions. now, with an explicit general delineation of the responsibilities of the ecb and national authorities, it must publish its administrative pecuniary sanction decisions and whether or not an appeal has been lodged and the time limits for enforcing sanctions are reduced. finally, i welcome the adoption of the socialist amendment which provides that the penalties paid by financial institutions should go to the single resolution fund in order to finance future crises in the sector.

in writing. — i have abstained on the vote regarding the overall modification of regulation (ec) 2532/98, concerning the powers of the european central bank to impose sanctions. although i consider positive many of the changes introduced, i disagree, alongside my political family, with the amendment that allows delaying publication of sanctions by the ecb until all legal recourses are exhausted. this notwithstanding, i am very satisfied that an amendment tabled by myself, proposing the transfer of sanctions proceeds related to the supervisory function of the ecb from this institution to the single resolution fund (srf), has passed with broad support political support, including the s&d, alde, gue and the greens. i hope the council will take on board this proposal, which will mobilise these proceeds for a concrete and productive purpose, increase the credibility and resources of the srf, and create a truly european funding source for it. it is a step forward for the banking union, and a more complete economic union.
in writing. - i think it is important to take advantage of today's debate to introduce a political and also democratic reflection on the nature of the ecb and its tasks in the monetary policy of the euro area. for example, who sets inflation targets and how? i believe that the european parliament, together with the council and the commission, should determine the recommended inflation rate. i also believe that the ecb should consult the council and the commission on the instruments to be used to raise current inflation, because we are running the risk of deflation and economic downturn for several dangerous years. it is clear - and i want to acknowledge this - that mr draghi is trying to stimulate domestic demand and facilitate credit, but there is still enormous resistance in the internal rules of the ecb and legitimate internal differences between national central banks in relation to these policies. is it not time to talk about a new statute for the central bank?
in writing. - i am satisfied with the outcome of this report and with the adoption of the amendment which states that 'the proceeds from sanctions imposed by the ecb in the exercise of its supervisory functions, including the collection of statistical information, will belong to the single resolution fund, which will be fed by the contributions of the banks themselves'. it is the financial institutions that should finance their potential crises, not the european citizens.

in writing. - parliament finally votes a resolution with a different undertone: the hope that lima will really be the prelude to a binding agreement that will allow us to put a stop to the climate emergency in paris. we cannot therefore accept amendment no 9 tabled by the ppe, which seeks to undermine two of the central pillars of the resolution by removing the requirement for binding targets also for energy efficiency and the promotion of renewable energies. we also reject the amendments tabled by the eug which seek to cast doubt on the effectiveness of the emissions trading system as a means of combating climate change at global and european level. we spanish socialists believe that the ets needs to correct its shortcomings, but it remains an excellent tool for achieving the common objectives of reducing greenhouse gases.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution on the lima climate summit. when we talk about climate negotiations, we move with hope, but we always end up with discouragement. we have to understand that this climate crisis that we're experiencing is a global crisis and it has to be our priority. and it is the capitalist logic of relocating production where there is less regulation that has led us into this crisis spiral. we should therefore not only be concerned about co2 emissions but also about the logic of market capitalism. to fight climate change, we should refuse to participate in this destructive race. this conference in lima should take a big step forward and adopt a binding global agreement.

mr president, the european steel industry has problems which require a common plan of action: the high energy costs, which are the result of liberalization in favour of private oligopolies, and the challenges arising from ecological adaptation, which cannot be solved by emission markets. but these problems must be seen in their true context, that of the disappearance of industrial policy under the cloak of competition policy. when the european coal and steel community was founded, it was to coordinate production and investment between the member states, to improve the welfare of workers and the autonomy of the european economy. it was a successful approach that inspired many to dream of europe. what's left of that today? the european commission uses its competition policy to reinforce market trends rather than exert control over them, forcing workers and states to compete with each other to lower wages and social standards, deindustrialising whole regions along the way. this is what happened to the steel industry and other sectors in my country, spain. this is not the way, commissioner. if we want to return to the european dream, competition policy must be subordinated to productive convergence and quality employment, a source of rights.
mr president, the steel sector in europe faces many challenges. one of them is the management of emission allowances, because we must continue to lead the fight against climate change, but we must fight for competitive prices for industry in order to offer a stable future to the sector. another central problem, which has to do with the foregoing, is the cost of electricity supply. steel, like much of industry, is energy intensive, and electricity prices have reached unsustainable levels in many member states. it is vital, alongside climate change policy and security of supply, to offer energy prices, competitive electricity prices to industry that do not represent an insurmountable obstacle. in this connection, in my country we have in recent days seen the result of a new mechanism for electricity pricing for energy-intensive industry. one of these companies, alcoa, has announced that the result of this new system may be the closure of its plants in spain, asturias and galicia. and we cannot assume that there are industries that have to leave europe because of mistakes in badly designed regulations. we ourselves expelled a good part of industry from europe. i therefore take advantage of this debate to say that i will not leave the workers of alcoa in avilés, lugo and a coruña alone, and that we will fight for the revision of this new system of electricity pricing for intensive industry. i trust that parliament will support all the initiatives i will take in the coming days.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the problem of hunger in the southern countries. but children in southern europe are also suffering from malnutrition. in my country, galicia, more than 20% of children live below the poverty line. in the spanish state, 60% more people are at risk of poverty and social exclusion today than in 2007. the cause of this situation is the policies of the european union, which make it possible for multinationals to steal the wealth of the people, which prevent them from developing their agriculture, which occupy their land, which impose free trade agreements that are ruinous for the people. without questioning these policies there will be no solution to hunger and malnutrition in the south, without putting an end to the troika policies hunger and malnutrition in the north will continue to advance. the european union's neoliberal policies must be radically changed, commissioner, by urgent measures such as putting an end to the predatory policies of the multinationals, ending free trade agreements, and adapting and changing agricultural and food policies within the framework of food sovereignty. anything less than progress in this direction will be empty words, and next year we will still be counting numbers of people who are malnourished, numbers of people who are starving to death.
mr president, i would like to thank you. thank you very much, mrs mcavan, for your excellent paper. talking about child malnutrition is no longer the exclusive privilege of developing countries. the figures for child poverty in large countries, in european countries such as my own, spain, are a source of shame and scandal. we are talking about three and a half million children who are not guaranteed adequate daily nutritional supply for their timely development, the physical and intellectual development that is essential to become first-class citizens, as we all strive for. how are we going to be able to work, to address and to end hunger in developing countries if we are able to allow this to be happening in the countries of the european union in 2015? you have mentioned agriculture, water and education for the developing countries. let me propose that we combine these issues with decent employment and nutritional and educational security, with universal child benefit in the countries of the european union. society must think about the future of children, but it is our obligation to act on their present. they have rights, but they don't have the capacity to enforce them, so it's up to us adults to defend them.
mr president, we do indeed proclaim and defend the right to food as a moral obligation. more than 165 million children under five are malnourished and approximately 52 million suffer from acute malnutrition. we are faced with an urgent challenge and an urgent need that must be met quickly. the initiative we are debating today is absolutely timely, very timely, and all the more so as this tuesday, in this very house, we voted with a very large majority 541 votes a resolution on the union and the global framework for development after 2015. the position of parliament, ladies and gentlemen, is unequivocally clear. we literally consider food to be a basic human right, in order to set a clear goal of zero hunger and end the hunger scandal by the year 2025 at the latest. we stress here that efforts to eradicate hunger, malnutrition and hidden hunger must focus especially on children and nursing mothers. i am very happy to note that in the united nations proposal for the new post-2015 development agenda one of the goals is to end all forms of malnutrition by the year 2030 by focusing on children. but we must open the field of vision more widely to achieve our goal and eradicate child malnutrition. efforts should be made to help developing countries improve in other areas, such as the provision of safe drinking water and sanitation, hygiene, sustainable agriculture, fisheries, the management of natural resources, the achievement of a healthy environment, measures to support women to ensure a healthy life for them and for all members of their households. in addition, family farming and its coherence with global land governance and tenure frameworks should be promoted.
mr president, i would first like to begin by acknowledging the role of the european union in development aid and the fight against child malnutrition. however, the food and financial crises since 2008 have caused these figures to rise again and put the achievement of the millennium development goals at risk. the commission's announcement of eur 3.5 billion to combat this situation is therefore a positive step, but more is needed. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of life in the regions of the community. in this multi-sectoral plan i would like to highlight three major objectives: the first objective, a programme of the first thousand days of a child, considered to be critical for their further development; the second, the promotion of small-scale agriculture; and, thirdly and no less importantly, the stimulation and promotion of women's participation in the distribution of resources, because it is clear and recognized that when women distribute resources within the family and control them, malnutrition within the family is much lower. so let's empower women, let's give them land ownership and let's educate women and girls.
mr president, with 3.1 million child deaths every year in developing countries, malnutrition is the leading cause of death in children under five. the fight against child malnutrition is and remains one of the main millennium development goals for 2015. when we talk about child malnutrition, we always link it to food insecurity and poverty, but also to unhealthy home environments and inadequate access to health services. today, 805 million people in the world do not have enough food to lead a healthy life, most of them in sub-saharan africa and also in asia. one in nine people in the world is in this situation. there are also 66 million school-age children in the world who go to school hungry. the first thousand days of a child's life are crucial - as has been said here - for the child to grow up fully and for his dignity to be respected. it is therefore considered the most critical period for preventing malnutrition and its consequences in adulthood. it is true that the european union has made a considerable effort in all areas of development cooperation, but we still have to do more to overcome this problem, with innovative financing, but also with long-term financing. the aim is to be able to talk about the availability of food, the accessibility of food and also to adapt food to the needs of the children themselves. we need to invest more in health, in education, but also in equal opportunities. a large proportion of women and children working in agriculture, if they had the same rights and had the same opportunities and access to services as men, would not be in this situation. i therefore encourage the commission and the commissioner to work along these lines. above all, political will is needed to invest in these areas.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, our group advocates secularism, that is, the separation of religion and state. in this way, we protect all religions. i repeat, we protect all religions. that is why we cannot but protest against these blasphemy laws, because they violate international human rights conventions. that is why we are calling on the pakistani government to abolish them in order to comply with all international law. and they have signed the international covenant on civil and political rights, the convention against torture and even a moratorium on the death penalty. but we must not forget that the growth of religious extremists has much to do with western interference: the use of these extremist groups, the destabilisation of baluchistan or the use, for our beloved nobel peace prize, of extrajudicial killing by means of unmanned aerial vehicles.
in writing. podemos will vote against this resolution on grounds of form and substance. the resolution is in line with article 135 of the european parliament's rules of procedure on statements 'on urgent cases of breaches of human rights, democracy and the rule of law'. the statements made by šešelj on the 23rd anniversary of vukovar, however incendiary they may have seemed to some, cannot be considered an urgent case to which article 135 applies. we believe that this article of the regulation should not be used in the particular interest of a member state, as might have happened in this case. furthermore, the resolution is one-sided and makes the responsibility of other parties to the conflict obvious by not mentioning the responsibility of gotovina, markač (also indicted by the international tribunal for the former yugoslavia for war crimes) or croatian paramilitary groups in the clashes in krajina or vukovar. the resolution also obviously condemns the ultra-nationalist and hateful statements that have been made in croatia. we can condemn any ultranationalist rhetoric that seeks to influence the political agenda of the region and hinders the reconciliation of the people of the former yugoslavia.
the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force. i miss to point out what happened in 2004, when the coalition authority repealed the 1959 civil code, the secular family statute - "the most advanced in the middle east" - that had emerged from the republican revolution, which granted rights to all women, regardless of their faith, and which was replaced by one that gave religious or tribal leaders the power to regulate family affairs through religious laws. i miss the condemnation of all actors, not just isis: iraqi government, multinational forces, military and security companies; as well as the demand to abolish in the laws all discrimination against women or the lgbt community. and so i think we are just going to abstain on this resolution.
